title: Dictionaries: looking things up by name
summary: Dictionaries as key-value pairs; creating, reading d[key], KeyError, adding and changing entries; in checks keys; get() with a default; keys(), values(), items() and looping; the counting pattern with a dictionary (frequency counts); finding the most common item.
text: Find it by name, not by position In real life Your phone's contacts. You never think "Mum is contact number 37". You search for "Mum" and get her number. The name is how you look things up; the number is what you find. A dictionary stores pairs: a key (the name you look up) and its value (what you find). It's written in curly braces, with a colon between each key and its value. 1 4 contacts.py phone = {"Mum": "0803 111 2222", "Ada": "0812 333 4444"} print(phone["Ada"]) phone["Bo"] = "0905 555 6666" # add a new pair phone["Mum"] = "0803 999 0000" # change an existing one print(len(phone)) Shows 0812 333 4444 3 Reading and writing use square brackets like lists, but with the key instead of a position. Writing to a key that doesn't exist yet adds it; writing to one that does replaces its value. Keys are unique: one value per key. Missing keys Look up a key that isn't there and you get a KeyError : phone["Zara"] gives KeyError: 'Zara' . 1 Two safe ways to ask: "Zara" in phone is True or False (it checks the keys). 2 phone.get("Zara", "unknown") gives the value if the key exists, otherwise the fallback, "unknown" . 3 New words Dictionary A collection of key-value pairs, written {"key": value} . Key What you look up. Each key appears once. Value Here: what a key leads to. KeyError The error when you look up a key that isn't in the dictionary. Try it: safe lookup Write capital_of(country) that returns the capital from the capitals dictionary, or "I don't know" if the country isn't in it. capitals = {"Nigeria": "Abuja", "Ghana": "Accra", "Kenya": "Nairobi"} def capital_of(country): return capitals[country] Going through a dictionary In real life Reading down a price list in a shop window: item, price; item, price. You can read just the item names, just the prices, or both together, line by line. Three methods give you the parts of a dictionary: 2 .keys() , .values() , and .items() , which gives each key and value together. With items() , the for line can unpack both into two names: prices.py prices = {"bread": 1200, "milk": 900, "eggs": 2500} for item, price in prices.items(): print(f"{item}: {price}") print(sum(prices.values())) Shows bread: 1200 milk: 900 eggs: 2500 4600 A plain for key in prices: loops over the keys. Dictionaries keep the order you added things in. Try it: what needs restocking? Write low_stock(stock, limit) that returns a list of the item names whose amount is below limit , in the dictionary's order. def low_stock(stock, limit): result = [] # your code here return result Counting with a dictionary In real life Counting votes on a whiteboard: each time a name is called out, you find it on the board and add a tally mark. If the name isn't on the board yet, you write it with one mark. That's the frequency count . You'll use it in several LeetCode problems in Lesson 20: votes.py votes = ["Ada", "Bo", "Ada", "Chi", "Ada", "Bo"] tally = {} for name in votes: if name in tally: tally[name] += 1 else: tally[name] = 1 print(tally) Shows {'Ada': 3, 'Bo': 2, 'Chi': 1} The if / else can be shortened with get : tally[name] = tally.get(name, 0) + 1 means "the current count, or 0 if there isn't one, plus 1". New words Frequency count A dictionary from each item to how many times it appears. Try it: letter counts Write letter_counts(word) that returns a dictionary of how many times each letter appears. letter_counts("banana") returns {"b": 1, "a": 3, "n": 2} . def letter_counts(word): counts = {} # your code here return counts Challenge: who won? Write winner(votes) that returns the name with the most votes. Build a tally first, then find the key with the biggest value (like finding the largest by hand in Lesson 9). There won't be ties in the tests. def winner(votes): pass Stuck? A hint Two loops. First loop: build tally . Second loop: for name, count in tally.items(): , keeping track of the best name so far and replacing it when a count is bigger. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. With ages = {"Ada": 21, "Bo": 30} , what is ages["Bo"] ? 30 21 "Bo" A KeyError Square brackets with a key give that key's value. 2. What does ages.get("Chi", 0) give if "Chi" isn't a key? 0 None A KeyError "Chi" get returns the fallback value when the key is missing, instead of raising an error. 3. What does "Ada" in ages check? Whether "Ada" is a key Whether "Ada" is a value Whether ages is a string Whether ages is empty in on a dictionary checks its keys. 4. After d = {} , d["x"] = 1 , d["x"] = 5 , what is d ? {'x': 5} {'x': 1, 'x': 5} {'x': 6} {'x': 1} Keys are unique. Writing to an existing key replaces its value. title: Tuples and sets
summary: Tuples as fixed, unchangeable sequences; tuple unpacking (multiple assignment) and swapping; returning several values from a function as a tuple; sets of unique items; add(), in, len(); removing duplicates with set(); set operations & | -; using a set to detect duplicates while looping.
concepts: swapping with a, b = b, a
text: Tuples: a fixed bundle In real life A map location is two numbers that belong together: latitude and longitude. You'd never change just one of them on its own; together they mean one place. A date of birth (day, month, year) is the same. A tuple is like a list written with round brackets instead of square ones, with one big difference: it can't be changed after it's made. It's immutable, like a string. 1 3 place.py lagos = (6.52, 3.38) print(lagos[0]) lat, lon = lagos # unpack into two variables print(f"Latitude {lat}, longitude {lon}") Shows 6.52 Latitude 6.52, longitude 3.38 The line lat, lon = lagos is unpacking : one name per item, filled in order. 1 You already did this with for item, price in prices.items() in Lesson 13. Two tuple tricks you'll use constantly Swapping. a, b = b, a swaps two variables in one line, no temporary variable needed. 2 Returning several values. A function can return smallest, largest . That returns one tuple, which the caller can unpack: low, high = min_max(numbers) . New words Tuple A fixed, unchangeable sequence: (6.52, 3.38) . Unpacking Giving each item of a sequence its own name: lat, lon = lagos . Try it: smallest and largest at once Write min_max(numbers) that returns a tuple of the smallest and largest numbers, in that order. You may use min() and max() . def min_max(numbers): pass Sets: each thing once In real life A sticker album: you either have a sticker or you don't. Getting the same sticker twice doesn't give you two places in the album. And checking whether you have one is instant: you go straight to its spot. A set holds unique items with no duplicates and no particular order. It's written with curly braces, but without the colons a dictionary has. It answers "is this in here?" very fast, even for huge sets. 4 stickers.py album = {"lion", "eagle"} album.add("shark") album.add("lion") # already there: no change print(len(album)) print("eagle" in album) print(set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])) # duplicates disappear Shows 3 True {1, 2, 3} Careful: {} on its own makes an empty dictionary . An empty set is written set() . 4 Comparing two sets Sets can be combined like circles in a diagram: 4 a & b (intersection): items in both. a | b (union): items in either. a - b (difference): items in a but not in b . New words Set An unordered collection of unique items: {"lion", "eagle"} . Intersection, union, difference In both, in either, in the first but not the second. Try it: friends in common Write in_common(friends_a, friends_b) that takes two lists of names and returns a sorted list of the names that appear in both. Use sets, then sorted() to turn the result into an ordered list. def in_common(friends_a, friends_b): pass The "seen before?" pattern In real life A doorman with a guest list who ticks off names as people arrive. If someone gives a name that's already ticked, he knows straight away that name was used twice, without re-reading the whole list. To find a repeat while going through a list, keep a set of everything you've seen so far. For each new item, check the set first, then add it. Because checking a set is fast, this is much quicker on big lists than comparing every item with every other item. That speed difference is exactly what Lesson 19 (Big O) is about, and this pattern solves LeetCode 217 in Lesson 20. Try it: first repeated item Write first_repeat(items) that returns the first item that appears for a second time while reading left to right, or None if nothing repeats. In ["a", "b", "c", "b", "a"] , it's "b" : the second b comes before the second a . def first_repeat(items): seen = set() # your code here return None Stuck? title: Debugging and testing your code
summary: Reading tracebacks with several frames from the bottom up; a table of common exceptions; a debugging method (reproduce, read, guess, check with print, fix, re-test); try/except for expected errors such as ValueError; raising exceptions; assert; testing edge cases (empty, zero, negative, single item, boundaries).
text: Reading a longer error In real life A parcel's tracking history: "collected in Lagos, sorted in Ibadan, damaged in Ilorin". The last line is where things went wrong; the lines above show the route it took to get there. When an error happens inside a function, Python's message, called a traceback , lists every function call on the way, oldest first ("most recent call last"). An error that happens while the program runs is called an exception . 1 report.py def average(numbers): return sum(numbers) / len(numbers) def report(scores): print(f"Average: {average(scores)}") report([]) Shows Traceback (most recent call last): File "report.py", line 7, in <module> report([]) File "report.py", line 5, in report print(f"Average: {average(scores)}") File "report.py", line 2, in average return sum(numbers) / len(numbers) ZeroDivisionError: division by zero (Newer versions of Python also draw ^ and ~ marks under the exact part of each line; they're left out here to keep it short.) Read from the bottom: what went wrong (division by zero), then where (line 2, in average ), then the route that led there ( report called average , the main program called report with an empty list). The real cause is often a few lines up the route: here, nobody expected an empty list. The usual suspects Error Usually means SyntaxError Code written wrongly: missing colon, bracket or quote IndentationError Block lines not indented as expected NameError A name used before it was given a value, often a typo TypeError Wrong kind of value, like adding text to a number ValueError Right kind of value, wrong content, like int("ten") IndexError A list position past the end KeyError A dictionary key that isn't there ZeroDivisionError Dividing by zero, often len() of something empty AttributeError A method that doesn't exist for that type, like [1, 2].upper() A calm way to hunt bugs In real life A mechanic doesn't replace random parts. They listen to the noise, make a guess ("probably the belt"), check that one thing, and only then fix it. Guessing and changing things at random makes it worse. Reproduce it. Find an input that makes the bug happen every time. Read the message , bottom up. If there's no error but the answer is wrong, compare what you expected with what you got. Make one guess about the cause. Check the guess by looking inside: print the variables at the suspicious point, for example print("DEBUG", i, total) inside a loop. Python's logging module is a tidier tool for bigger programs, but a temporary print is the quickest start. 5 Fix it , remove the debug prints, and re-test every case, not just the one that failed. Try it: find the bug count_above(numbers, limit) should return how many numbers are greater than limit . It gives wrong answers. Press Check , compare expected and got, add a debug print if it helps, and fix it. def count_above(numbers, limit): count = 0 for i in range(1, len(numbers)): if numbers[i] > limit: count += 1 return count Stuck? A hint Which test fails? It's the one where the big number is first. Print i inside the loop: which index never appears? Handling the errors you expect In real life A trapeze artist works with a safety net. They don't plan to fall, but if they do, the net catches them and the show goes on. Some errors aren't bugs; they're things you know might happen, like a person typing "ten" when you asked for a number. try / except is the safety net: Python tries the risky code, and if that kind of error happens, it runs the except block instead of crashing. 2 3 ask_age.py while True: try: age = int(input("Age? ")) break except ValueError: print("Please type a whole number.") print(f"Thanks, {age}.") Shows (typed ten, then 21) Age? ten Please type a whole number. Age? 21 Thanks, 21. Name the specific error after except , as above. A bare except: catches everything, including your own typos, and hides real bugs. You can also cause an exception on purpose with raise , when your function receives something it can't sensibly handle: raise ValueError("age can't be negative") . 4 Try it: safe_int Write safe_int(text) that returns the whole number in text , or None if it isn't one. Use try / except ValueError . def safe_int(text): return int(text) Testing your own code: edge cases In real life Testing a new bridge, engineers don't just drive one normal car over it. They try the heaviest lorry, an empty bridge in a storm, and traffic jammed bumper to bumper. An edge case is an unusual but valid input at the extremes. Most bugs hide there. Before you call a function finished, try: Empty : an empty list, an empty string. One item : a list with a single number. Zero and negatives . Boundaries : exactly 18 when the rule says "18 or over" (Lesson 5). Duplicates and ties . A quick way to write your own tests is assert : a line that does nothing when its condition is true, and stops the program with an AssertionError when it's false. 4 Put a few under your function in a .py file: test_average.py assert average([2, 4]) == 3 assert average([5]) == 5 assert average([]) == 0 print("All tests passed") LeetCode does the same thing on a bigger scale: it runs your function against hidden edge cases. Thinking of them yourself first is how you get "Accepted" on the first submit. New words Exception An error that happens while the program is running. Traceback Python's report of an exception and the chain of calls that led to it. try / except Run risky code, and handle a named error instead of crashing. assert A check that stops the program if its condition is false. Edge case An extreme but valid input, like an empty list. Try it: survive the edge cases Fix average(numbers) so it returns 0 for an empty list instead of crashing, and still works for everything else. def average(numbers): return sum(numbers) / len(numbers) Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. In a traceback, which line names the kind of error? The very last line The very first line The longest line The line with File The last line names the error. The lines above show the route of calls that led there. 2. [1, 2, 3][5] raises which error? IndexError KeyError ValueError TypeError Index 5 is past the end of a 3-item list. 3. Why name the error in except ValueError: instead of a bare except: ? So unexpected bugs aren't hidden Because bare except is a SyntaxError So the program runs faster Because ValueError is the only error A bare except also catches mistakes you didn't expect, like typos, and silently hides them. 4. Which is the best edge case to test for a function that averages a list? An empty list A list of three numbers A list of even numbers A list of small numbers An empty list makes len() zero, which would divide by zero. That's an extreme the normal cases never touch. title: Nested loops and grids
summary: Nested loops (a loop inside a loop) and how many times the inner block runs; grids as lists of lists; grid[row][col]; number of rows and columns; list comprehensions for building lists and grids; the [[0] * n] * m trap; checking bounds; counting the 8 neighbours of a cell; transposing a grid.
text: A loop inside a loop In real life A clock: for every one step of the hour hand, the minute hand goes all the way round. Or an usher checking tickets: for each row of the cinema, go along every seat in that row, then move to the next row. Put a loop inside another loop's block and you get a nested loop . The inner loop runs completely, from start to finish, for every single step of the outer loop: seats.py for row in ["A", "B"]: for seat in range(1, 4): print(f"{row}{seat}", end=" ") print() # finish the row's line Shows A1 A2 A3 B1 B2 B3 Two small new things: print(..., end=" ") ends with a space instead of a new line, so the seats stay on one line, and an empty print() just starts a new line. How many times does the inner block run? Outer count times inner count: 2 rows times 3 seats is 6. Keep that multiplication in mind; it becomes important when we talk about speed in Lesson 19. Grids as lists of lists In real life A spreadsheet: you find a cell by its row and then its column. "Row 2, column 3." A noughts-and-crosses board is a 3 by 3 grid of the same kind. A grid is stored as a list whose items are themselves lists: one inner list per row. 2 Two indexes find a cell: first the row, then the column. board.py board = [ ["X", "O", "X"], [" ", "X", "O"], ["O", " ", "X"], ] print(board[0][2]) # row 0, column 2 print(len(board)) # number of rows print(len(board[0])) # number of columns for row in board: print(" | ".join(row)) Shows X 3 3 X | O | X | X | O O | | X To visit every cell with its position, loop over the row numbers and, inside, the column numbers: for r in range(len(board)): and for c in range(len(board[0])): , then use board[r][c] . Building lists the short way A list comprehension builds a list in one line: [n * n for n in range(5)] gives [0, 1, 4, 9, 16] . Read it as "n times n, for each n in range(5)". 1 It's the same as an empty list plus a for loop with append , just shorter. For grids, it's the safe way to make one: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)] makes 2 rows of 3 zeros. ( _ is a name programmers use for a loop variable they don't need.) The shared-row trap The tempting shortcut [[0] * 3] * 2 looks the same but isn't: it makes one row and puts it in the grid twice. Change a cell in one row and the "other" row changes too, because they're the same list. 3 Always build grids with a comprehension or a loop. Try it: a times-table grid Write times_grid(n) that returns an n by n grid where the cell at row r, column c holds (r + 1) * (c + 1) . times_grid(3) returns [[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], [3, 6, 9]] . def times_grid(n): grid = [] # your code here return grid Stuck? A hint Outer loop over r : start an empty row . Inner loop over c : append the product to row . After the inner loop, append row to grid . Try it: flip a grid Write transpose(grid) that returns a new grid whose rows are the original's columns (LeetCode 867). [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] becomes [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]] . def transpose(grid): pass Stuck? A hint The new grid has one row for each column of the old one. So the outer loop goes over column numbers, and the inner loop collects grid[r][c] for every row r . Counting a cell's neighbours In real life Standing on one square of a chessboard, the squares touching yours are up, down, left, right and the four diagonals: up to 8. But if you're on the edge, some of those squares don't exist: you'd be stepping off the board. Many grid problems, including Conway's Game of Life (your project in Lesson 36 4 ), need the cells around a given cell. The neat way is to loop over the row offsets -1, 0, 1 and column offsets -1, 0, 1, skip the (0, 0) offset (that's the cell itself), and skip any position that falls off the grid. That last check is called bounds checking : bounds.py def in_bounds(grid, r, c): return 0 <= r < len(grid) and 0 <= c < len(grid[0]) Without it, row -1 would wrap round to the last row (negative indexes count from the end), and there's no error message to warn you. New words Nested loop A loop inside another loop's block. Grid A list of lists, one inner list per row: grid[row][col] . List comprehension A one-line list builder: [x * 2 for x in nums] . Bounds checking Making sure a position is inside the grid before using it. Transpose Swap a grid's rows and columns. Try it: live neighbours Write live_neighbours(grid, r, c) that returns how many of the up-to-8 cells around (r, c) hold 1 . Don't count the cell itself, and don't step off the edge. def live_neighbours(grid, r, c): count = 0 for dr in [-1, 0, 1]: for dc in [-1, 0, 1]: pass # your code here return count Stuck? A hint Inside the inner loop: skip when both offsets are 0 ( continue ). Work out nr = r + dr and nc = c + dc . If they're in bounds, add grid[nr][nc] to count (it's 1 or 0). Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. An outer loop runs 4 times and an inner loop 5 times. How many times does the inner block run? 20 9 5 4 The inner loop runs fully for every outer step: 4 times 5. 2. With g = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]] , what is g[2][0] ? 5 2 3 6 Row 2 is [5, 6], and column 0 of that row is 5. 3. What does [n + 1 for n in [1, 2, 3]] give? [2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3, 1] [1, 2, 3] [3, 4, 5] It takes each n and puts n + 1 in the new list. 4. Why is [[0] * 3] * 3 a bad way to make a grid? All three rows are the same list It makes a grid of ones It raises a TypeError It only makes one row The outer * 3 repeats a reference to one row, so changing one row changes them all. You'll build it in Lesson 36, and today's neighbour function is the hardest part. Tomorrow, before Lesson 17 In practice/grid_sum.py , from memory: write row_sums(grid) returning a list of each row's total, and column_sums(grid) returning each column's total. Test them with assert lines. Stuck? Ask your tutor With the course app running, press Ask your tutor . A good question for today: "can you trace a nested loop for me step by step?"

title: Classes and objects
summary: Classes as blueprints and objects (instances) made from them; __init__ and self; attributes; methods; calling methods on objects; strings and lists as objects; LeetCode's class Solution wrapper and why self is there; a Node class with a value and a link to the next node as a preview of linked lists.
text: Blueprints and the things made from them In real life A cookie cutter isn't a cookie. It's the shape you use to make as many cookies as you like. Each cookie is separate: you can put icing on one without changing the others, but they all share the same shape. A class is the cookie cutter: a blueprint describing what data a kind of thing holds and what it can do. An object (also called an instance ) is one cookie made from it. 1 You've used objects already: every string is an object of the class str , which is why it has methods like .upper() . pets.py class Dog: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name self.tricks = [] def learn(self, trick): self.tricks.append(trick) def show_off(self): return f"{self.name} can: {', '.join(self.tricks)}" rex = Dog("Rex") bella = Dog("Bella") rex.learn("sit") rex.learn("roll over") print(rex.show_off()) print(len(bella.tricks)) Shows Rex can: sit, roll over 0 Taking it apart class Dog: starts the blueprint. Class names use CapitalisedWords by convention. Dog("Rex") makes a new object. Python then runs __init__ (two underscores each side, said "dunder init") to set it up. 2 self means "this particular object". Inside the class, self.name is this dog's name. When you call rex.learn("sit") , Python passes rex in as self automatically. 3 self.name and self.tricks are attributes : variables that belong to one object. Rex's tricks and Bella's tricks are separate lists. learn and show_off are methods : functions that belong to the class, with self as their first parameter. New words Class A blueprint for a kind of object. Object / instance One thing made from a class: Dog("Rex") . __init__ The method that sets up a new object. self Inside a class, the particular object being used. Attribute A variable that belongs to an object: rex.name . Try it: a click counter Write a class Counter . A new counter starts with a count attribute of 0. Its method click() adds 1, and reset() puts it back to 0. class Counter: def __init__(self): pass Getting "has no attribute 'count'"? Inside __init__ , write self.count = 0 . Without self. , count would be a local variable that's wiped when __init__ finishes (Lesson 12). Try it: a bank account Write BankAccount(owner) with a balance starting at 0. deposit(amount) adds money. withdraw(amount) takes it out and returns True , but if there isn't enough money it changes nothing and returns False . class BankAccount: def __init__(self, owner): self.owner = owner self.balance = 0 LeetCode's class Solution, explained In real life An exam paper with a box marked "Write your answer here". The box is just where the examiner knows to look. LeetCode's class Solution is that box. LeetCode wraps every answer as a method of a class called Solution . Its test system makes an object, Solution() , and calls your method on it with each test input. That's why there's a self parameter you never use: every method gets one. 3 So writing for LeetCode means: write your function as you normally would, then indent it inside class Solution: and add self as the first parameter. Solve it: LeetCode 1480, Running Sum Inside class Solution , write runningSum(self, nums) that returns a list where each item is the total of all numbers up to and including that position. [1, 2, 3, 4] gives [1, 3, 6, 10] . 4 class Solution: def runningSum(self, nums): pass Stuck? A hint The accumulator pattern from Lesson 8, with one extra step: after adding each number to total , append the current total to the result list. A preview: objects that point to objects In real life A treasure hunt: each clue tells you something and also where to find the next clue. You can follow the whole chain from the first clue, one step at a time, until a clue says "the end". An attribute can hold another object. A tiny class with a value and a link to the next one is the building block of a linked list , which you'll study in Lesson 27: clues.py class Node: def __init__(self, val, next=None): self.val = val self.next = next third = Node("under the mat") second = Node("in the oven", third) first = Node("behind the clock", second) clue = first while clue is not None: print(clue.val) clue = clue.next Shows behind the clock in the oven under the mat is not None asks "is there actually a node here?". The last node's next is None , so the loop stops there. Read that loop slowly; you'll write lots like it. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What does self refer to inside a method? The object the method was called on The class blueprint itself The first argument you passed The whole running program In rex.learn("sit"), Python passes rex as self. 2. When does __init__ run? When a new object is created When the class is written Whenever any method is called When the program finishes Calling the class, like Dog("Rex"), creates an object and runs __init__ to set it up. 3. a = Counter() and b = Counter() , then a.click() . What is b.count ? 0 1 2 None Each object has its own attributes. Clicking a doesn't change b. 4. Why do LeetCode methods have a self parameter? They're methods of a Solution class LeetCode needs your username there It stores the expected answer It makes the code run faster Every method's first parameter is the object it's called on. LeetCode calls Solution().yourMethod(...). Read, then practise from memory Read next The Python Tutorial, 9.3 A First Look at Classes About 20 minutes. It's written for experienced programmers, so read for the examples and skip any paragraph that loses you. Sections 9.3.1 to 9.3.5 are the useful part. title: Modules, pip and virtual environments
summary: import and modules; the standard library (math, random); from ... import; your own module files; if __name__ == "__main__"; packages from PyPI installed with pip; virtual environments with python -m venv .venv; running .venv\Scripts\python directly; ModuleNotFoundError when a package isn't installed in the environment you're using.
text: Borrowing tools with import In real life You don't forge your own hammer before hanging a picture; you take one from the toolbox. Python's toolbox is called the standard library, and import is how you take a tool out. A module is a file of ready-made Python code. import loads one so you can use what's inside, written as module_name.thing . 1 2 Modules that come with every Python installation are called the standard library . tools.py import math import random print(math.sqrt(81)) # square root print(math.pi) print(random.randint(1, 6)) # a dice roll: 1 to 6, both included print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"])) Shows something like 9.0 3.141592653589793 4 paper Unlike range , random.randint(1, 6) includes both ends. 4 The last two lines show different results each run; that's the point of random . If you only need one thing, from math import sqrt lets you write sqrt(81) without the math. in front. Try it: the long side of a triangle Write hypotenuse(a, b) that returns the square root of a * a + b * b , using math.sqrt . For sides 3 and 4 it returns 5.0 . def hypotenuse(a, b): pass Try it: roll the dice Write roll(sides=6) that returns a random whole number from 1 to sides . The tests roll it hundreds of times to check every result is in range and every face shows up. import random def roll(sides=6): pass Your own modules In real life A cook who keeps their best sauce recipes in a separate notebook can use them in any meal, instead of rewriting them inside every recipe. Any .py file is a module. If shapes.py sits in the same folder as main.py , then main.py can say import shapes and use shapes.area(3, 4) . 2 This is how real projects stay organised: one file per topic. One line you'll see at the bottom of many Python files: shapes.py def area(width, height): return width * height if __name__ == "__main__": print(area(3, 4)) # runs only when you run shapes.py directly It means "only run this part if this file was run directly, not imported". 3 It's the right place for quick tests of a module's functions. Installing packages, safely In real life A carpenter takes a separate toolbox to each job, packed with exactly what that job needs. Tools for one client's kitchen never get mixed up with another client's garden shed. Beyond the standard library, people share hundreds of thousands of packages on PyPI, the Python Package Index. pip is the tool that downloads and installs them. 6 A virtual environment is the separate toolbox: a folder holding its own copy of Python and its own installed packages, usually one per project, so projects don't interfere with each other. 5 Next you'll make one and install a small, silly package called cowsay . Make a project folder and the environment. In the terminal, from your course folder: Terminal ...python-course> mkdir practice\cow python-course % mkdir -p practice/cow python-course $ mkdir -p practice/cow ...python-course> cd practice\cow python-course % cd practice/cow python-course $ cd practice/cow ...cow> python -m venv .venv cow % python3 -m venv .venv cow $ python3 -m venv .venv This creates a hidden-looking folder called .venv with its own Python inside. It takes a few seconds and prints nothing. On Ubuntu or Debian, if it says ensurepip is not available , run sudo apt install python3-venv and try again. Install a package into it. Use the environment's own Python to run pip: Terminal ...cow> .venv\Scripts\python -m pip install cowsay cow % .venv/bin/python -m pip install cowsay cow $ .venv/bin/python -m pip install cowsay The official tutorial also shows "activating" an environment so plain python python3 uses it. 5 On Windows PowerShell that can be blocked by a security setting, so this This course uses .venv\Scripts\python .venv/bin/python directly instead. It always works and you can always see which Python you're using. Use it. Terminal ...cow> .venv\Scripts\python -c "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('Hello from my venv')" cow % .venv/bin/python -c "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('Hello from my venv')" cow $ .venv/bin/python -c "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('Hello from my venv')" Shows __________________ | Hello from my venv | ================== \ \ ^__^ (oo)\_______ (__)\ )\/\ ||----w | || || See the toolbox wall. Now try the same with the ordinary python python3 : Terminal ...cow> python -c "import cowsay" cow % python3 -c "import cowsay" cow $ python3 -c "import cowsay" Shows ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cowsay' That's not a failure: it proves the package lives only in this project's environment. Whenever you see ModuleNotFoundError in a project, the first question is "am I using the right environment's Python?" Paste the last line the ordinary python showed: Exactly right. The package is inside .venv only, which is what you want. If it printed nothing, cowsay was installed globally by accident. If you got an error at step 2, paste it to your tutor. New words Module A file of Python code you can import . Standard library The modules that come with Python, like math and random . Package Shared code you install from PyPI with pip. pip The tool that installs packages: python python3 -m pip install name . Virtual environment A project's own folder of Python and packages, usually .venv . Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. Which numbers can random.randint(1, 3) return? 1, 2 or 3 1 or 2 only 0, 1 or 2 Any decimal number randint includes both ends, unlike range. 2. After from math import sqrt , how do you call it? sqrt(16) math.sqrt(16) import sqrt(16) math(sqrt, 16) from ... import brings the name in directly, so you don't need the math. prefix. 3. Your project shows ModuleNotFoundError for a package you installed. Most likely cause? The wrong Python is running it The package is broken forever The file name is too long Python needs reinstalling first Packages live in one environment. Run your code with that environment's Python, like .venv\Scripts\python .venv/bin/python . 4. When does the code under if __name__ == "__main__": run? When the file is run directly When the file is imported Every time, no matter what Never, it's only a comment It's skipped when another file imports this one, so it's a safe spot for quick tests. title: Big O: how code slows down as data grows
summary: Measuring an algorithm by how its number of steps grows with input size n; O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2) with everyday examples; dropping constants and smaller terms; nested loops multiply, loops one after another add; worst case; space complexity; costs of common Python operations (in on a list is O(n), in on a set or dict is O(1) on average); replacing a nested-loop duplicate check with a set.
concepts: cost of list in vs set in
text: Same answer, very different wait In real life You need the word "python" in a paper dictionary. Method one: read every page from the start until you find it. Method two: open it in the middle, see you're at "m", jump halfway into the second half, and keep halving. Both find the word. For a thin dictionary the difference doesn't matter. For a 2,000-page one, method one could take hours and method two about a dozen flips. An algorithm is a step-by-step method for solving a problem. To compare algorithms, we don't time them with a stopwatch (that depends on the computer). We ask: as the input gets bigger, how fast does the number of steps grow? 1 The size of the input is called n : the number of items in the list, the length of the string. Big O notation is the shorthand for that growth. "This is O(n)" (said "oh of n") means "the steps grow in step with n: double the data, double the work". 1 The five shapes you'll meet most Big O Name In real life Steps for n = 1,000,000 O(1) constant Looking up a contact by name: same effort however many contacts you have 1 O(log n) logarithmic The dictionary halving trick, or guessing a number with "higher / lower" hints about 20 O(n) linear Reading every page once 1,000,000 O(n log n) "n log n" A good sorting method (Lesson 26) about 20,000,000 O(n²) quadratic Everyone at a party shaking hands with everyone else 1,000,000,000,000 Look at the last column. At a million steps a second, O(n) finishes in one second. O(n²) would take about eleven days. That's why interviewers care: on big inputs, the shape matters far more than how fast the computer is. 1 Why is halving O(log n)? Each step throws away half of what's left. A million items halve to one item in about 20 steps, because 2 multiplied by itself 20 times is just over a million. 4 Working out the Big O of code In real life Estimating a journey, you care whether it's a walk to the shop or a drive across the country. Whether you stop for one minute or two at the traffic lights doesn't change the answer. Three rules cover most code: A loop over n items is O(n). Each step inside the loop that takes a fixed amount of work counts as O(1). Nested loops multiply. A loop over n inside a loop over n is n times n: O(n²) (remember the nested loops in Lesson 16). Loops one after another add : O(n) + O(n) is still O(n). Drop constants and smaller parts. 3n + 10 steps is O(n). n² + n is O(n²). Big O only describes the shape of the growth when n is huge, where those details stop mattering. 1 We also usually describe the worst case : searching a list for something that isn't there checks every item, so it's O(n), even though sometimes you get lucky on the first item. The same idea applies to memory, called space complexity : a function that builds a set of all n items uses O(n) extra space; one that only keeps a running total uses O(1). Hidden loops Some single lines hide a loop. The big one for interviews: 2 3 x in my_list checks items one by one: O(n) . x in my_set and key in my_dict jump straight to the spot: O(1) on average. my_list.append(x) is O(1), but my_list.insert(0, x) (put x at the front) and my_list.pop(0) (take the first item out) shift every other item along: O(n). sorted(my_list) is O(n log n). So a loop containing if x in some_list is secretly a nested loop: O(n²). Swap the list for a set and it becomes O(n). You'll use that speed-up often in interview answers. Try it: count the steps Make the growth visible. linear_steps(n) should loop over range(n) and return how many times its body ran. pair_steps(n) should loop over range(n) inside another loop over range(n) and return how many times the inner body ran. Then press Run to see the table the last lines print. def linear_steps(n): steps = 0 # one loop here return steps def pair_steps(n): steps = 0 # a loop inside a loop here return steps for n in [10, 100, 1000]: print(n, linear_steps(n), pair_steps(n)) Your first speed-up Here's a correct but slow way to check a list for duplicates: compare every item with every later item. Two nested loops over n: O(n²). slow.py def has_duplicate_slow(items): for i in range(len(items)): for j in range(i + 1, len(items)): if items[i] == items[j]: return True return False On a list of 20,000 different numbers, that's about 200 million comparisons. The "seen before?" set from Lesson 14 does it in one pass: O(n) time, using O(n) extra space for the set. The last test uses 20,000 items: the slow version would be stopped after 6 seconds; yours should finish instantly. def has_duplicate(items): pass New words Algorithm A step-by-step method for solving a problem. Space complexity How the extra memory an algorithm uses grows with n. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. A function loops once over a list of n items, doing a fixed amount of work each time. Its Big O? O(n) O(1) O(n²) O(log n) One pass over n items is linear. 2. Simplify 4n² + 3n + 7 in Big O. title: Arrays and hashing: remember what you've seen
summary: Hash tables (Python's dict and set) give O(1) average lookups; the pattern of trading O(n) extra space for O(n) time; LeetCode 217 Contains Duplicate, 242 Valid Anagram (character counts), 1 Two Sum (store each number's index, look up the complement), 49 Group Anagrams (dictionary keyed by sorted letters).
text: Why dictionaries are so fast In real life A cloakroom: you hand over your coat and get ticket number 47. When you come back, the attendant doesn't search every hook; they walk straight to hook 47. The ticket number tells them exactly where to look. Python's dict and set are built on a hash table . When you store a key, Python runs it through a hash function that turns it into a number, and that number says which slot to put it in. Looking it up later repeats the calculation and goes straight to the slot, instead of searching. 1 That's why key in my_dict is O(1) on average (Lesson 19). In LeetCode problems, a Python list is usually called an array . The pattern for this lesson: The hash map pattern. If the slow answer is "for each item, search the rest of the list", walk the list once instead, and keep a set or dictionary of what you've seen so the search becomes an O(1) lookup. You spend O(n) memory to save a whole factor of n in time. Each exercise uses LeetCode's exact class Solution format (Lesson 17), so once the tests pass you can paste it straight into LeetCode and submit. LeetCode 217: Contains Duplicate Return True if any value appears at least twice in nums , and False if every value is different. 4 You did this in Lesson 19; write it again from memory in LeetCode's format. class Solution: def containsDuplicate(self, nums): pass A one-line version Once yours passes: return len(set(nums)) != len(nums) also works. A set drops duplicates, so if it's shorter than the list, something repeated. Same O(n), but it can't stop early. Counting characters In real life Two bags of Scrabble tiles spell different words, "listen" and "silent". Are they the same tiles? Tip each bag out and count: three E's? two N's? If every letter count matches, the bags are interchangeable. An anagram uses exactly the same letters in a different order. Sorting both words and comparing works, but sorting is O(n log n). Counting each word's letters into a dictionary (Lesson 13) and comparing the dictionaries is O(n). 2 LeetCode 242: Valid Anagram Return True if t is an anagram of s . 5 The words contain lowercase letters only. class Solution: def isAnagram(self, s, t): pass Stuck? A hint Simplest O(n) version: build a letter-count dictionary for each word (the get(ch, 0) + 1 trick from Lesson 13), then return counts_s == counts_t . Dictionaries compare equal when they have the same keys and values. Two Sum In real life You're at a party and need a partner whose age adds to yours to make exactly 50. You're 20, so you need someone who's 30. Instead of asking everyone their age again and again, there's a register at the door listing everyone who's arrived and their age. You just check: "is anyone 30 on the list?" Given a list of numbers and a target , find the positions of the two numbers that add up to it. The slow way tries every pair: O(n²). The hash map way walks the list once. For each number, the partner you need is target - number , called the complement . Check whether the complement is already in a dictionary of numbers you've seen (mapping number to index). If it is, you're done. If not, add the current number and carry on. 6 trace.txt nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9 i=0 num=2 need 7 seen={} not there, store 2 -> 0 i=1 num=7 need 2 seen={2: 0} found at 0! answer [0, 1] LeetCode 1: Two Sum Return a list of the two indexes, smaller first. Each input has exactly one answer, and you can't use the same item twice. class Solution: def twoSum(self, nums, target): seen = {} # number -> its index # your code here Hint 1: you need the index too Loop with for i in range(len(nums)): and num = nums[i] . Python also has for i, num in enumerate(nums): , which hands you both at once; that's the tidy way. Hint 2: order of the two steps Check for the complement before storing the current number. Otherwise [3, 3] with target 6 could match a number with itself. Challenge: a clever key In real life Sorting post into pigeonholes: each letter goes into the hole labelled with its postcode. Letters with the same postcode end up together without you ever comparing two letters directly. To group anagrams, you need a label that's the same for every word in a group. Sorting a word's letters gives exactly that: "eat", "tea" and "ate" all become "aet". Use that as a dictionary key and put each word in the list for its key. "".join(sorted(word)) turns the sorted letters back into a string. LeetCode 49: Group Anagrams Return a list of groups (lists of words) where each group is a set of anagrams. The groups and the words inside them can be in any order. 7 class Solution: def groupAnagrams(self, strs): groups = {} # your code here return list(groups.values()) # list() turns the groups into a plain list New words Array LeetCode's word for a list of values. Hash table The structure behind dict and set: a key's hash says which slot it lives in. Complement In Two Sum, the number you still need: target - num . enumerate() Gives each item together with its index: for i, x in enumerate(items) . Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What's the Big O of the hash map Two Sum? O(n) time, O(n) space O(n²) time, O(1) space O(1) time, O(n) space O(log n) time, O(1) space One pass with O(1) lookups is O(n) time; the dictionary can hold up to n numbers. 2. In Two Sum with target 10, you're at the number 4. What do you look up? 6 4 14 10 The complement is target minus the current number: 10 - 4. 3. Why are "listen" and "silent" given the same key in Group Anagrams? Sorted, both letters spell eilnst They have the same first letter They both have six characters Python treats them as equal Sorting the letters gives the same string for every anagram. 4. When is the hash map pattern a good idea? When you'd otherwise search inside a loop When the list is already sorted When memory is extremely limited When the list has one item A search inside a loop is O(n²); a set or dict lookup turns it into O(n), using extra memory. title: Two pointers
summary: The two-pointer pattern: left and right indexes moving towards each other; swapping in place; skipping characters with str.isalnum(); using the sorted order to decide which pointer to move; LeetCode 344 Reverse String, 125 Valid Palindrome, 167 Two Sum II, 11 Container With Most Water.
concepts: moving the pointer using sorted order
text: Two people walking towards each other In real life Two friends stand at opposite ends of a bridge and walk towards the middle, checking the railings as they go. When they meet, the whole bridge has been checked, and nobody walked it twice. In this pattern, a pointer is just a variable holding an index. You keep two: left starting at 0 and right starting at the last index. Each step, you look at both items, do something, and move one or both pointers inwards. When they meet, you've visited every item once: O(n) time, and only two extra variables, so O(1) extra space. 1 3 shape.py left, right = 0, len(items) - 1 while left < right: # look at items[left] and items[right] left += 1 right -= 1 Changing a list directly, instead of building a new one, is called working in place . LeetCode 344: Reverse String Reverse the list of characters s in place (change the list itself; don't return anything) using two pointers and swaps. 4 No [::-1] and no .reverse() . class Solution: def reverseString(self, s): pass Stuck? A hint The swap trick from Lesson 14 works on list items too: s[left], s[right] = s[right], s[left] . Do that, move both pointers, repeat while left < right . Skipping what doesn't count In Lesson 10 you checked palindromes by building a cleaned, reversed copy: O(n) extra memory. Two pointers do it with none. The twist in LeetCode 125: ignore everything that isn't a letter or digit, and ignore capitals. "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" is a palindrome. 5 ch.isalnum() is True when a character is a letter or a digit. 2 When a pointer is on a space or punctuation mark, move it past without comparing. LeetCode 125: Valid Palindrome Return True if s reads the same forwards and backwards, considering only letters and digits and ignoring case. Use two pointers, not a reversed copy. class Solution: def isPalindrome(self, s): left, right = 0, len(s) - 1 # your code here return True Stuck? A hint Inside while left < right: handle one situation per step with if / elif : left isn't alphanumeric, move left; right isn't, move right; lowercased characters differ, return False ; otherwise move both. When the list is sorted In real life Paying exactly 1,000 with one note and one coin from a tray sorted smallest to biggest. Try the smallest with the biggest. Too much? The biggest can't work with anything, so put it back. Too little? The smallest can't work with anything, so drop it. Each try rules one item out for good. LeetCode 167 is Two Sum on a sorted list. Start pointers at both ends and add the two values. Too big: move right left to get a smaller number. Too small: move left right to get a bigger one. Equal: done. Each step rules out one number forever, so it's O(n) with no dictionary at all. 6 Note this problem counts positions from 1, not 0. LeetCode 167: Two Sum II numbers is sorted from smallest to largest. Return the 1-based positions [index1, index2] of the two numbers that add up to target , using O(1) extra space. class Solution: def twoSum(self, numbers, target): pass Challenge: Container With Most Water Each number is the height of a vertical line. Pick two lines; with the floor they make a container. The water it holds is the distance between them times the shorter line. Find the most water. 7 Start with the widest container (both ends). To possibly do better you must find a taller short side, so move the pointer at the shorter line inwards. Moving the taller one can never help: the width shrinks and the short side stays the limit. LeetCode 11: Container With Most Water Return the maximum amount of water. [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7] gives 49 (lines at positions 1 and 8: width 7, height 7). class Solution: def maxArea(self, height): pass Stuck? A hint Keep a best variable. Each step: work out the water for the current pair with min() , update best , then move whichever pointer has the shorter line. New words Pointer Here: a variable holding an index into a list or string. In place Changing the original list instead of building a new one. isalnum() True if a string is all letters and digits. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What extra space does Reverse String with two pointers use? O(1): just two indexes O(n): a reversed copy O(n²): a grid of swaps O(log n): halving each time Swapping in place needs only the two pointer variables. 2. Two Sum II: the two pointed-at numbers add up to more than the target. What do you do? Move the right pointer left Move the left pointer right Move both pointers inwards Restart from the beginning The list is sorted, so moving right gives a smaller number and a smaller sum. 3. Why does Two Sum II's two-pointer trick need the list to be sorted? To know which way makes the sum smaller So the answer is always at the ends Because unsorted lists can't be indexed So duplicates are removed first Sorted order tells you which pointer to move. Unsorted, that decision means nothing. 4. What is "a1!".isalnum() ? False True "a1" 2 It's True only if every character is a letter or digit; "!" is neither. title: Sliding window
summary: The sliding window pattern for contiguous subarrays and substrings; fixed-size windows updated by adding the new item and removing the old; tracking the best so far (minimum price) in one pass; variable-size windows with a set that grow on the right and shrink on the left; LeetCode 121 Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, 643 Maximum Average Subarray I, 3 Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters.
text: Remember the best so far In real life Looking back over a month of a share's price, you want the biggest profit from buying on one day and selling on a later day. You don't need to compare every pair of days. Walk forward day by day remembering one thing: the cheapest price so far. Each day, ask "if I'd bought at that cheapest point and sold today, what would I make?" That's LeetCode 121. 3 Comparing every buy day with every later sell day is O(n²). Keeping the lowest price seen so far makes it one pass, O(n), with O(1) extra space. It's the simplest version of this lesson's idea: as you move along, keep a small summary of what's behind you instead of looking back. LeetCode 121: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock prices[i] is the price on day i . Return the most profit from one buy followed by one later sell, or 0 if no profit is possible. class Solution: def maxProfit(self, prices): lowest = prices[0] best = 0 # your code here return best Stuck? A hint For each price: first update lowest if today is cheaper. Then work out today's profit, price - lowest , and keep it if it beats best . A window of fixed size In real life A train window shows exactly four fields at a time. As the train moves, one new field appears on the right and one disappears on the left. To keep a running total of cows in view, you don't recount everything: add the cows in the new field, subtract the cows in the one that left. A contiguous stretch of a list (items next to each other, no gaps) is called a subarray ; in a string it's a substring . A sliding window is a subarray you move along one step at a time. 1 For a window of size k , summing each window from scratch costs O(n·k). Sliding costs O(n): add the item entering on the right, subtract the item leaving on the left. slide.txt nums = [1, 12, -5, -6, 50, 3], k = 4 first window [1, 12, -5, -6] sum 2 slide: +50 -1 [12, -5, -6, 50] sum 51 slide: +3 -12 [-5, -6, 50, 3] sum 42 LeetCode 643: Maximum Average Subarray I Return the largest average of any k neighbouring numbers in nums . 4 Find the largest window sum by sliding, then divide by k once at the end. class Solution: def findMaxAverage(self, nums, k): window = sum(nums[:k]) best = window # slide the window from position k onwards return best / k Stuck? A hint Loop for i in range(k, len(nums)): . The item entering is nums[i] ; the one leaving is nums[i - k] . Update window , then best = max(best, window) . A window that grows and shrinks In real life A caterpillar crawling along a leaf: its head stretches forward, and when it gets uncomfortable, its tail catches up. It's never longer than it can comfortably be, and it never goes backwards. LeetCode 3 asks for the longest substring with no repeated characters. 5 Keep a window from left to the current position right , and a set of the characters inside it. Move right forward one character at a time. If the new character is already in the window, shrink from the left (removing characters from the set) until it isn't. Then add it and check the length. Each character is added once and removed at most once, so even with the inner while loop, the total work is O(n). 2 caterpillar.txt s = "abcabcbb" right=0 'a' window "a" best 1 right=1 'b' window "ab" best 2 right=2 'c' window "abc" best 3 right=3 'a' 'a' is inside: drop 'a' from the left -> "bca" right=4 'b' 'b' is inside: drop 'b' -> "cab" ... best stays 3 LeetCode 3: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters Return the length of the longest substring of s with all different characters. class Solution: def lengthOfLongestSubstring(self, s): window = set() left = 0 best = 0 for right in range(len(s)): pass # your code here return best Hint 1: shrinking while s[right] in window: remove s[left] from the set and move left forward. Sets have .remove() , the opposite of .add() . Hint 2: the window's length After adding s[right] , the window runs from left to right inclusive, so its length is right - left + 1 . New words Contiguous Next to each other, with no gaps. Subarray / substring A contiguous piece of a list / of a string. Sliding window A subarray that moves along, updated rather than recomputed. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. A window of size k slides one step right. How do you update its sum? Add the new item, subtract the old Add up all k items again Multiply the old sum by k Subtract the new, add the old Only two items change, so updating is O(1) per step instead of O(k). 2. In Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, what do you track as you go? The lowest price so far The highest price so far Every pair of prices The average price so far The best sale today always uses the cheapest earlier buy. 3. Why is LeetCode 3 O(n) even with a while loop inside the for loop? Each character leaves the window once The while loop never actually runs Sets make every loop O(1) The string is always short left only moves forward, so across the whole run the inner loop does at most n removals in total. 4. Which of these is a contiguous subarray of [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] ? [1, 4, 1] [3, 4, 5] [5, 1, 4] [3, 1, 5] Contiguous means neighbouring items in their original order, with no gaps. title: Stacks: last in, first out
summary: The stack: push and pop at one end only, last in first out (LIFO); a Python list as a stack with append() and pop() and peeking with [-1]; checking an empty stack; LeetCode 20 Valid Parentheses with a dictionary of closing-to-opening brackets; 155 Min Stack keeping a second stack of minimums; 150 Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, including division that truncates towards zero with int(a / b).
text: Only the top plate In real life A stack of plates in a canteen. You put clean plates on top, and you take plates from the top. The plate washed last is the first one used. Getting the bottom plate means lifting off every plate above it. A stack is a collection where you only add and remove at one end, the top. Adding is called push , removing is pop , and looking at the top without removing it is peek . The last item pushed is the first popped: LIFO , last in, first out. 1 A Python list is already a good stack: append() pushes onto the end, pop() removes and returns the last item, and stack[-1] peeks. 4 All three are O(1). Popping an empty list raises IndexError: pop from empty list , so check first: an empty list counts as false, so if stack: means "if there's anything on it". undo.py history = [] history.append("type hello") history.append("make bold") history.append("delete line") print(history.pop()) # undo the last action print(history[-1]) # what would be undone next Shows delete line make bold Matching brackets In real life Russian dolls: each doll you open must be closed before the doll around it. You can't close the big doll while a small one inside is still open. The most recently opened doll is always the next one to close: a stack. In "([{}])" , every closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening one. Push each opening bracket. When a closing bracket arrives, the top of the stack must be its partner: pop it. If the stack is empty or the top doesn't match, the string is invalid. At the end, the stack must be empty: any leftovers were never closed. 2 A dictionary from each closing bracket to its opener keeps the code short: pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"} . LeetCode 20: Valid Parentheses Return True if every bracket in s is closed by the right kind, in the right order. 5 class Solution: def isValid(self, s): pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"} stack = [] # your code here Stuck? A hint For each character: if it's a closing bracket ( ch in pairs ), the stack must be non-empty and its top must equal pairs[ch] ; then pop. Otherwise push it. At the end, return len(stack) == 0 . A stack that knows its minimum LeetCode 155 wants a stack class whose getMin() is O(1), with no searching. 6 The trick: keep a second stack alongside. Every time you push a value, also push "the smallest value so far" onto the second stack. Pop both together. The second stack's top is always the current minimum. A second structure that exists only to help the main one is often called an auxiliary stack. LeetCode 155: Min Stack Write the class MinStack with push(val) , pop() , top() (returns the top value) and getMin() . Every method must be O(1). class MinStack: def __init__(self): self.stack = [] self.mins = [] def push(self, val): pass def pop(self): pass def top(self): pass def getMin(self): pass Challenge: maths without brackets In real life Old pocket calculators worked like this: type the two numbers first, then the operation. "3, 4, plus" gives 7. Numbers wait on a pile until an operation comes along and combines the top two. In Reverse Polish Notation (postfix), the operator comes after its two numbers: ["2", "1", "+", "3", "*"] means (2 + 1) × 3 = 9. No brackets are ever needed. Evaluate it with a stack: push numbers; on an operator, pop two, combine, push the result. 3 Watch the order: the first number popped is the right -hand one. For "10", "2", "-" you pop 2, then 10, and compute 10 - 2. LeetCode also wants division that cuts off the decimal towards zero: int(a / b) does that (6 / -4 gives -1, not -2). 7 LeetCode 150: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation tokens is a list of strings: numbers and the operators + - * / . Return the result as an int. class Solution: def evalRPN(self, tokens): stack = [] # your code here Careful with negative numbers "-11" is a number, not an operator. Checking t in "+-*/" is safe because "-11" in "+-*/" is False : the whole string has to appear inside. New words Stack A collection you add to and remove from at the top only. Push / pop / peek Add to the top / remove from the top / look at the top. LIFO Last in, first out. Reverse Polish Notation Maths with each operator after its two numbers. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. Push 1, push 2, push 3, then pop. Return False: wrong partner Pop it and keep going Push the closing bracket Skip it and check later The most recent opener must match. A [ closed by ) is invalid. 3. title: Binary search
summary: Binary search on a sorted list: low, high and mid = (low + high) // 2; floor division //; while low <= high; moving low = mid + 1 or high = mid - 1; O(log n); returning -1 when missing; LeetCode 704 Binary Search, 35 Search Insert Position (low ends at the insert point), and 69 Sqrt(x), searching over possible answers instead of a list.
text: Halve it, every time In real life "I'm thinking of a number from 1 to 100." Guess 50. "Higher." Now it's 51 to 100, so guess 75. "Lower." 51 to 74: guess 62. Each guess throws away half of what's left, so you never need more than 7 guesses for 100 numbers, or about 20 for a million. Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by checking the middle and discarding the half that can't hold it. 1 Each step halves the search area, so it's O(log n), compared with O(n) for checking items one by one (Lesson 19). You keep two indexes, low and high , marking the part still in play, and compute the middle with mid = (low + high) // 2 . The // operator is floor division : it divides and drops the decimal part, so 7 // 2 is 3 . 2 An index must be a whole number. trace.txt nums = [-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], target = 9 low=0 high=5 mid=2 nums[2]=3 too small -> low = 3 low=3 high=5 mid=4 nums[4]=9 found at 4 The three details that trip everyone up while low <= high , with "or equal". When low == high there's still one item left to check. Move past mid : low = mid + 1 or high = mid - 1 . You've already checked mid ; keeping it can make the loop run forever. Sorted only. On an unsorted list the "throw away half" step throws away the answer. LeetCode 704: Binary Search Return the index of target in the sorted list nums , or -1 if it isn't there. 3 It must be O(log n): the last test uses two million numbers and is checked thousands of times. class Solution: def search(self, nums, target): low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1 # your code here return -1 Stuck? A hint Inside while low <= high: find mid . Three cases: equal, return mid ; middle value too small, the answer is to the right, so low = mid + 1 ; too big, high = mid - 1 . Where would it go? In real life Filing a new folder in an alphabetical cabinet. Even if no folder has that name yet, the search tells you where it belongs: between the last folder before it and the first after it. When binary search fails, low isn't random: it stops at the exact position where the target would be inserted to keep the list sorted. That's all LeetCode 35 asks for. 4 LeetCode 35: Search Insert Position Return the index of target if it's in the sorted list, otherwise the index where it would be inserted. class Solution: def searchInsert(self, nums, target): pass Stuck? A hint It's your 704 solution with one change: what you return after the loop. Challenge: binary search without a list Binary search works on anything where "too small" and "too big" make sense in order. LeetCode 69 asks for the whole-number part of a square root, without using math.sqrt or ** 0.5 . 5 The possible answers 0, 1, 2, ..., x are already in sorted order, so search them : for a guess mid , if mid * mid is too big, go lower; otherwise go higher. Keep track of the last guess whose square fitted. This idea, called binary search on the answer , shows up in many Medium and Hard problems. LeetCode 69: Sqrt(x) Return the square root of x rounded down to a whole number, using binary search. mySqrt(8) is 2 (because 2 × 2 = 4 fits but 3 × 3 = 9 is too big). class Solution: def mySqrt(self, x): low, high = 0, x answer = 0 # your code here return answer Stuck? A hint If mid * mid <= x , mid could be the answer: save it, then look higher with low = mid + 1 . Otherwise look lower. New words Binary search Searching a sorted range by repeatedly checking the middle and discarding half. Floor division // Division that drops the decimal part: 7 // 2 is 3. Binary search on the answer Searching a sorted range of possible answers rather than a list. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. About 20 About 1,000 About 500,000 About 1,000,000 Halving a million down to one takes about 20 steps: O(log n). 2. nums[mid] is smaller than the target. What next? low = mid + 1 high = mid - 1 low = mid high = mid The target must be to the right, and mid itself is already ruled out. 3. What is 17 // 5 ? 3 3.4 2 4 Floor division drops the decimal part of 3.4. 4. What does binary search require of its input? It must be sorted It must have no duplicates It must have an even length It must contain the target Discarding half only works if order tells you which half can't hold the answer. title: Recursion: functions that call themselves
summary: Recursion as solving a problem using a smaller version of itself; the base case and the recursive case; the three laws of recursion; the call stack and stack frames; RecursionError and the recursion limit; factorial, sum of a list, reversing a string, power; LeetCode 509 Fibonacci and why plain recursive Fibonacci is exponentially slow.
text: A smaller copy of the same problem In real life You're in a long queue at the cinema and want to know your position. You ask the person in front: "what number are you?" They don't know either, so they ask the person in front of them, and so on, until the question reaches the first person, who just says "1". Then the answers travel back: "2", "3", ... until someone tells you, and you add one. Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. 1 Every recursive function needs two parts: a base case : a version so small the answer is obvious (the first person in the queue says "1"), and a recursive case : do a little work and call yourself on something smaller (ask the person in front, then add one). factorial.py def factorial(n): if n == 0: # base case return 1 return n * factorial(n - 1) # recursive case print(factorial(4)) # 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 Shows 24 The textbook calls these the three laws of recursion : have a base case; move towards it on every call; call yourself. 2 Break the second law (forget the - 1 ) and the calls never stop. How Python keeps track: the call stack In real life Reading a book that says "see page 40", which says "see page 72". You keep a finger in each page so you can come back. When page 72 is done, you return to 40, finish it, then return to where you started. Your fingers form a stack: the last page you marked is the first you return to. Each time a function is called, Python puts a stack frame on the call stack : a note holding that call's local variables and where to return to. 3 4 For factorial(4) , four frames pile up (4, 3, 2, 1) above the base case. Then they finish in reverse order, each multiplying the answer from below. It's a stack, just like Lesson 23. unwinding.txt factorial(4) = 4 * factorial(3) factorial(3) = 3 * factorial(2) factorial(2) = 2 * factorial(1) factorial(1) = 1 * factorial(0) factorial(0) = 1 = 1 = 2 = 6 = 24 The stack can't grow forever. Python stops at about 1,000 frames by default and raises RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded . 5 If you see that, your function almost certainly never reaches its base case. Try it: sum a list recursively Write sum_list(numbers) without loops and without sum() . Base case: an empty list sums to 0. Recursive case: the first number plus the sum of the rest, numbers[1:] . def sum_list(numbers): pass Try it: reverse a string recursively Write reverse(text) with no loops and no slicing with [::-1] . Think: the reverse of "abc" is the reverse of "bc", followed by "a". def reverse(text): pass Stuck? A hint Base case: the reverse of "" is "" . Recursive case: reverse(text[1:]) + text[0] . Fibonacci, and a warning In real life Asking two friends to each work out half of a problem, and they each ask two friends, who each ask two more. The question spreads like a family tree, and most of those people end up working out the exact same sub-question as somebody else. The Fibonacci numbers start 0, 1, and each next one is the sum of the two before: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13... That definition is already recursive: fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) , with base cases fib(0) = 0 and fib(1) = 1 . 6 Written that way it's correct but very slow: each call makes two more calls, so the work roughly doubles with every step of n. That's exponential time, O(2ⁿ): fib(30) makes over a million calls, and fib(50) would take hours. The fix is to remember answers you've already worked out, which is the whole idea of dynamic programming in Lesson 33. For now, LeetCode only asks up to n = 30 , so the plain version is accepted. LeetCode 509: Fibonacci Number Return the nth Fibonacci number using recursion. class Solution: def fib(self, n): pass Inside a class, call it as self.fib A method calls another method (or itself) through self : self.fib(n - 1) . Plain fib(n - 1) gives a NameError. New words Recursion A function solving a problem by calling itself on a smaller version. Base case The smallest version, answered directly, which stops the calls. Call stack Python's stack of unfinished function calls, one frame per call. RecursionError The error when the call stack gets too deep, usually a missing base case. Exponential time Work that roughly doubles each time n grows by one, like O(2ⁿ). Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What stops a recursive function from calling itself forever? Reaching its base case Python's for loop limit The return value being None Running out of variables The base case returns without calling itself again, so the calls can finish. 2. You see RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded . Most likely cause? The base case is never reached The list is already sorted A variable name has a typo The function returns a string Each call adds a frame; without reaching the base case, they pile up past the limit. 3. Why is plain recursive Fibonacci slow? It re-computes the same values many times Adding numbers is slow in Python Recursion is always slower than loops It uses floating-point numbers fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2) both recompute the same smaller values again and again. 4. With def f(n): return 0 if n == 0 else n + f(n - 1) , what is f(3) ? 6 3 0 9 3 + 2 + 1 + 0. (This one-line form, A if condition else B, is called a conditional expression.)
