title: Sorting
summary: Why simple sorts like insertion sort are O(n^2); merge sort as divide and conquer: split in half, sort each half recursively, merge two sorted lists with two pointers, O(n log n); Python's sorted() and list.sort(); sorting with key= functions, reverse=True, and tuples for tie-breaks; stable sorting; LeetCode 88 Merge Sorted Array (merge from the back) and 912 Sort an Array with merge sort.
text: Sorting a hand of cards In real life Picking up playing cards one at a time: each new card gets slid left past the bigger ones until it sits in the right place among the cards you already hold. That's easy with 7 cards, but with a whole shoe of 300, each new card has to be compared with lots of others. That's insertion sort : take each item and move it left until it's in place among the sorted items before it. 1 In the worst case, each of the n items slides past up to n others: O(n²). Most "obvious" sorting methods are O(n²) for the same reason: they compare items close to every other item. Try it: insertion sort Finish insertion_sort(items) so it sorts the list in place and returns it. For each position i , take items[i] and shift bigger items in front of it one place right until you find its spot. def insertion_sort(items): for i in range(1, len(items)): current = items[i] j = i - 1 # while j is in range and items[j] is bigger than current: # move items[j] one place right, and step j left # then put current at position j + 1 return items Merge sort: divide and conquer In real life A teacher with 64 exam papers to put in name order gives half to each of two assistants, who each split theirs again, until everyone holds one paper (already "sorted"). Then pairs combine: two neat piles merge into one by repeatedly taking whichever top paper comes first. Piles double in size until one sorted stack is left. Merge sort is a divide and conquer algorithm: split the list in half, sort each half (recursively, Lesson 25), then merge the two sorted halves. 2 The base case: a list of 0 or 1 items is already sorted. The merge step is two pointers (Lesson 21): one at the start of each sorted half. Repeatedly take the smaller of the two front items, and when one half runs out, add the rest of the other. Why it's fast: halving gives about log n levels of splitting, and each level does O(n) work merging, so O(n log n) in total. 2 For a million items that's about 20 million steps instead of a trillion. Step 1: merge two sorted lists Write merge(a, b) that takes two sorted lists and returns one sorted list with all their items, using two pointers (no sorted() ). def merge(a, b): result = [] i, j = 0, 0 # while both lists still have items, take the smaller front item # then add whatever is left over return result Adding the leftovers After the loop, one list may still have items. result.extend(a[i:]) adds everything left in a (it adds nothing if a is used up); do the same for b . extend is like append for a whole list of items. Step 2: LeetCode 912, Sort an Array, with merge sort Write sortArray(self, nums) as a merge sort. Split at mid = len(nums) // 2 , sort both halves with self.sortArray , then merge them (paste your merge into the class as a helper method, or keep it as a function above the class). 6 def merge(a, b): pass # paste your merge from step 1 class Solution: def sortArray(self, nums): pass Stuck? A hint Three lines after the base case: left = self.sortArray(nums[:mid]) , right = self.sortArray(nums[mid:]) , return merge(left, right) . Trust that the recursive calls return sorted halves. In real code: sorted() and key In real life A class register can be sorted by surname, by age, or by exam score. The students are the same; what changes is which detail you compare. In real code and in most interviews (unless they ask you to implement one), use Python's built-in sort, which is O(n log n). 3 sorted(items) returns a new sorted list; items.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None . The key argument says what to compare: a function applied to each item. reverse=True sorts biggest first. register.py words = ["banana", "Kiwi", "apple", "fig"] print(sorted(words, key=len)) print(sorted(words, key=str.lower)) def by_score(student): return student[1] students = [("Ada", 72), ("Bo", 91), ("Chi", 72)] print(sorted(students, key=by_score, reverse=True)) Shows ['fig', 'Kiwi', 'apple', 'banana'] ['apple', 'banana', 'fig', 'Kiwi'] [('Bo', 91), ('Ada', 72), ('Chi', 72)] Notice Ada stays before Chi: they tie on 72, and Python's sort is stable , meaning items that compare equal keep their original order. 4 To sort by two things, return a tuple from the key: key=by_age_then_name returning (age, name) sorts by age, and by name where ages tie. Try it: a leaderboard Write leaderboard(players) . players is a list of (name, score) tuples. Return the names ordered by score, highest first; where scores tie, alphabetical order by name. def leaderboard(players): pass Stuck? A hint A key returning (-score, name) sorts by score descending (the minus flips it) and then by name ascending. Then build the list of names with a list comprehension (Lesson 16). Challenge: merging from the back LeetCode 88 gives two sorted lists, but the first one, nums1 , has extra zeros on the end making room for the second, and you must merge in place into nums1 . 5 Merging from the front would overwrite items you haven't used yet. The trick: fill from the back. Compare the largest remaining items of each list and write the bigger one into the last empty slot. LeetCode 88: Merge Sorted Array nums1 has m real items followed by n zeros; nums2 has n items. Change nums1 in place so it holds all m + n items sorted. Don't return anything. class Solution: def merge(self, nums1, m, nums2, n): i, j, write = m - 1, n - 1, m + n - 1 # your code here Stuck? A hint Loop while j >= 0 (items of nums2 left to place). If nums1 still has items and its biggest is bigger, write it at write ; otherwise write nums2[j] . Move the pointer you used, and write , one step left. Leftover nums1 items are already in place. New words Divide and conquer Split a problem into halves, solve each, and combine the answers. Merge sort Sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves. O(n log n). Key function A function telling sorted() what to compare for each item. Stable sort A sort that keeps equal items in their original order. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What is the Big O of merge sort? O(n log n) O(n²) O(n) O(log n) About log n levels of halving, with O(n) merging work on each level. 2. What does nums.sort() return? None A new sorted list The original list unchanged The smallest item list.sort() sorts in place and returns None. sorted() is the one that returns a new list. 3. What does sorted(["bb", "a", "ccc"], key=len) give? ['a', 'bb', 'ccc'] ['ccc', 'bb', 'a'] [1, 2, 3] ['bb', 'a', 'ccc'] key=len compares the lengths, but the items themselves are what's returned. 4. In Merge Sorted Array, why fill nums1 from the back? The back is empty, so nothing is overwritten Big numbers are easier to compare LeetCode reads the answer backwards It makes the algorithm O(log n) The spare slots are at the end, so writing there never destroys an item you still need. title: Linked lists
summary: Linked lists of ListNode objects with val and next; head and None at the end; walking a list with cur = cur.next; why inserting at the front is O(1) but indexing is O(n); reversing by re-pointing next with prev/cur; a dummy head node to simplify building a new list; fast and slow pointers for the middle and for cycle detection (Floyd's algorithm). LeetCode 206, 21, 876, 141.
text: A chain of nodes In real life A train where each carriage is only coupled to the one behind it. To reach carriage 8 you walk through carriages 1 to 7; there's no shortcut. But adding a new carriage at the front is quick: couple it on and call it the front. No other carriage has to move. A linked list is a chain of nodes . Each node holds a value ( val ) and a link to the next node ( next ); the last node's next is None . You only hold on to the first node, called the head . 1 LeetCode calls the node class ListNode . chain.txt head | v [1 | next] -> [2 | next] -> [3 | next] -> None Compared with a Python list: 2 getting item number k means walking k steps, O(n). But adding at the front is O(1) (make a node whose next is the old head), where list.insert(0, x) is O(n). Interviewers mostly use linked lists to test whether you can move pointers around without losing the chain. Walking the list, called traversal , always looks the same: walk.py cur = head while cur is not None: print(cur.val) cur = cur.next In the exercises below, a ListNode class and two helpers are already written for you (open "Already written for you" to see them): build([1, 2, 3]) makes a chain from a Python list, and to_list(head) turns a chain back into a Python list so the tests can compare. Try it: count the nodes Write length(head) that returns how many nodes are in the chain, by walking it. def length(head): count = 0 # your code here return count Reversing a linked list In real life A line of people each pointing at the person ahead of them. To reverse the line, walk along it and turn each person round to point at the person who was behind them. You need to remember who was behind (so they can be pointed at) and who's next (so you don't lose the rest of the line when someone turns round). Keep two pointers: prev (starts as None ) and cur (starts at the head). At each node: save cur.next before you lose it, point cur.next back at prev , then move both one step forward. When cur runs off the end, prev is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) extra space. 3 steps.txt start: None 1 -> 2 -> 3 prev cur step 1: None <- 1 2 -> 3 prev cur step 2: None <- 1 <- 2 3 prev cur step 3: None <- 1 <- 2 <- 3 None prev cur -> return prev LeetCode 206: Reverse Linked List Reverse the list and return the new head. class Solution: def reverseList(self, head): prev, cur = None, head # your code here return prev Stuck? A hint Inside while cur is not None: four lines, in this order: nxt = cur.next , cur.next = prev , prev = cur , cur = nxt . Merging, with a dummy head In real life Building a chain of paper clips, it's awkward to start because there's nothing to hook the first clip onto. So you hang a spare clip on a nail first and build from that. At the end you take the chain off the spare. LeetCode 21 merges two sorted linked lists into one, like the merge step of merge sort (Lesson 26). 4 Building a new chain means "attach to the end of what you've built", but at the start there's no end to attach to. A dummy node solves it: make dummy = ListNode() , keep a tail pointer at the end of your chain, attach nodes to tail.next , and at the end return dummy.next . LeetCode 21: Merge Two Sorted Lists Merge list1 and list2 into one sorted list by re-linking their nodes, and return its head. class Solution: def mergeTwoLists(self, list1, list2): dummy = ListNode() tail = dummy # your code here return dummy.next Stuck? A hint While both lists have nodes: attach the smaller front node to tail.next , advance that list, then tail = tail.next . Afterwards, attach whichever list still has nodes: tail.next = list1 or list2 works because None counts as false. Fast and slow pointers In real life Two runners start together; one runs twice as fast. On a straight track, when the fast one reaches the finish, the slow one is exactly halfway. On a circular track, the fast runner eventually laps the slow one and they meet again. Move slow one node per step and fast two. Two classic uses: The middle: when fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle (LeetCode 876). 5 Cycle detection: if a node's next points back to an earlier node, the list loops forever. If fast ever lands on the same node as slow , there's a cycle; if fast reaches None , there isn't (LeetCode 141, known as Floyd's algorithm). 6 O(1) extra space, where a "seen" set would need O(n). The loop condition protects you from stepping off the end: while fast is not None and fast.next is not None: . LeetCode 876: Middle of the Linked List Return the middle node. With two middles (an even number of nodes), return the second one. class Solution: def middleNode(self, head): slow = fast = head # your code here return slow LeetCode 141: Linked List Cycle Return True if the list has a cycle. Use fast and slow pointers, O(1) extra space. (The setup's build_cycle(values, pos) links the last node back to position pos ; -1 means no cycle.) class Solution: def hasCycle(self, head): slow = fast = head # your code here return False Comparing nodes: is To ask "are these the very same node object?", use slow is fast . Two different nodes could hold the same value, so comparing .val isn't enough. New words Linked list A chain of nodes, each holding a value and a link to the next. Head The first node of a linked list. Dummy node A placeholder node before the real start, making building a list simpler. Fast and slow pointers Two pointers moving at different speeds, to find the middle or a cycle. is Checks whether two names refer to the exact same object. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What's the cost of getting the 1000th value of a linked list? O(n): walk node by node O(1): jump straight there O(log n): halve each time O(n²): compare every pair There's no index; you follow next links from the head. 2. Reversing a list, why save cur.next before changing it? Otherwise the rest of the list is lost Python requires a temporary variable To make the code run in O(1) So the values can be compared Once cur.next points backwards, nothing points to the remaining nodes unless you saved them. 3. When fast reaches the end, where is slow ? In the middle At the start One node behind fast At the end too It has moved half as far. 4. What does the dummy node in Merge Two Sorted Lists give you? Something to attach the first node to A spare value for comparisons The smallest value in both lists A way to detect cycles With a dummy, every node, even the first, is attached the same way; you return dummy.next. title: Trees and depth-first search
summary: Binary trees of TreeNode objects with val, left and right; root, leaf, child, parent, depth; recursion on trees with the empty tree (None) as base case; depth-first search; preorder, inorder and postorder traversals; LeetCode 104 Maximum Depth, 100 Same Tree, 226 Invert Binary Tree, 94 Binary Tree Inorder Traversal; O(n) time and O(h) call-stack space.
text: Branching instead of a chain In real life A family tree drawn upside down: one ancestor at the top, their children below, and their children's children below that. Or the folders on your computer: a drive holds folders, which hold folders, which hold files at the bottom. A tree is made of nodes joined by links, starting from one node at the top called the root . In a binary tree , each node has at most two children , left and right . A node with no children is a leaf . The depth (or height) of a tree is the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. 1 2 tree.txt 3 <- root / \ 9 20 / \ 15 7 <- 9, 15 and 7 are leaves depth = 3 (3 -> 20 -> 15) LeetCode writes trees as a list read level by level, with None for a missing child: the tree above is [3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7] . In the exercises, build_tree turns such a list into TreeNode objects, and tree_to_list turns a tree back into one. Every subtree is a tree In real life To count everyone in a family tree, the head of the family can say: "it's me, plus everyone in my first child's branch, plus everyone in my second child's branch." Each child answers the same question about their own branch. Someone with no children just says "one". A node's left child is the root of a smaller tree (its subtree ), and so is its right child. So almost every tree problem has the same recursive shape: 1 shape.py def solve(node): if node is None: # base case: the empty tree return ... left_answer = solve(node.left) right_answer = solve(node.right) return ...combine node.val, left_answer and right_answer... Going all the way down one branch before coming back up to try the next is called depth-first search (DFS). It visits each node once: O(n) time. The extra space is the call stack, as deep as the tree is tall. LeetCode 104: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree Return the depth of the tree. The empty tree ( None ) has depth 0. A node's depth is 1 plus the deeper of its two subtrees. 4 class Solution: def maxDepth(self, root): pass Stuck? A hint Two lines: if root is None , return 0. Otherwise return 1 + max(left depth, right depth) , where each depth is self.maxDepth(...) of a child. LeetCode 100: Same Tree Return True if trees p and q have the same shape and the same values. 5 class Solution: def isSameTree(self, p, q): pass Stuck? A hint Base cases first: both None means same; exactly one None , or different values, means not the same. Otherwise both left subtrees must match and both right subtrees must match. LeetCode 226: Invert Binary Tree Mirror the tree: swap every node's left and right children, all the way down, and return the root. 6 class Solution: def invertTree(self, root): pass Three orders for visiting a tree In real life Reading out a family tree, you could announce each parent before their children (top-down), or the children before the parent (bottom-up), or the left-hand family, then the parent, then the right-hand family. A depth-first traversal visits every node, in one of three standard orders depending on when you record the node itself: 3 Preorder : node, then left subtree, then right subtree. Inorder : left subtree, then node, then right subtree. Postorder : left subtree, then right subtree, then node. For the tree [1, 2, 3] (1 at the root, 2 on the left, 3 on the right): preorder is 1, 2, 3; inorder is 2, 1, 3; postorder is 2, 3, 1. Yes, that's allowed. visit can see result because it's defined inside the method. Base case: if node is None: return . Then visit left, append node.val , visit right. Notice the last test: that tree is a binary search tree , where everything on a node's left is smaller and everything on its right is bigger. Inorder traversal of a binary search tree comes out sorted. That property is behind many tree interview questions. New words Binary tree A tree where each node has at most a left and a right child. Root / leaf The top node / a node with no children. Subtree A node and everything below it: itself a tree. Depth-first search (DFS) Exploring all the way down one branch before backing up to the next. Preorder / inorder / postorder When the node is visited: before, between, or after its subtrees. title: Queues and breadth-first search
summary: Queues as first in, first out (FIFO); why list.pop(0) is O(n) and collections.deque with append() and popleft() is O(1); breadth-first search on a tree level by level, processing len(queue) nodes per level; LeetCode 102 Binary Tree Level Order Traversal, 199 Binary Tree Right Side View, 111 Minimum Depth (BFS stops at the first leaf).
text: First come, first served In real life A queue at the bank: new people join at the back, and the person at the front is served next. Unlike a stack of plates, whoever has waited longest goes first. A queue adds at the back and removes from the front: FIFO , first in, first out. 1 You could use a list, but list.pop(0) shifts every remaining item along one place, so it's O(n). 2 Python's collections.deque (say "deck") is built for this: append() adds at the back and popleft() removes from the front, both O(1). 3 bank.py from collections import deque queue = deque(["Ada", "Bo"]) queue.append("Chi") # Chi joins the back print(queue.popleft()) # Ada is served first print(list(queue)) # list() copies the queue into a plain list for printing Shows Ada ['Bo', 'Chi'] Breadth-first search: level by level In real life Drop a stone in a pond: the ripple reaches everything one step away, then everything two steps away, then three. Or spreading news: you tell your friends, they tell their friends, and so on. Everyone at distance 1 hears before anyone at distance 2. Breadth-first search (BFS) visits nodes in order of how far they are from the start. 4 On a tree that means level by level: the root, then its children, then grandchildren. The queue makes it work: take a node from the front, then add its children to the back. Children always wait behind everyone already queued at the level above. To know where one level ends, look at the queue's length at the start of each level: that many nodes belong to this level. Process exactly that many, and anything added meanwhile is the next level. levels.py queue = deque([root]) while queue: level_size = len(queue) for _ in range(level_size): node = queue.popleft() # ...use node... if node.left: queue.append(node.left) if node.right: queue.append(node.right) # one whole level is done here DFS (Lesson 28) is natural with recursion; BFS is natural with a queue. Both visit each node once: O(n). Choose BFS when "nearest first" matters. LeetCode 102: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal Return the values level by level, as a list of lists: for [3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7] , that's [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]] . 5 from collections import deque class Solution: def levelOrder(self, root): if root is None: return [] result = [] queue = deque([root]) # your code here return result Stuck? A hint Use the shape above. At the start of each level make an empty level list, append each node's value to it inside the for , and after the for append level to result . LeetCode 199: Binary Tree Right Side View Standing to the right of the tree, which values can you see, top to bottom? That's the last node of each level. 6 from collections import deque class Solution: def rightSideView(self, root): pass Why BFS finds the shortest Because BFS reaches everything at distance 1 before anything at distance 2, the first time it finds what it's looking for, it has found the closest one. LeetCode 111 asks for the minimum depth: the number of nodes from the root down to the nearest leaf. 7 DFS would have to explore every branch to be sure. BFS can stop at the very first leaf it meets. LeetCode 111: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree Return the number of nodes on the shortest path from the root to a leaf. Use BFS and return as soon as you take a leaf off the queue. A node with only one child is not a leaf. from collections import deque class Solution: def minDepth(self, root): if root is None: return 0 queue = deque([(root, 1)]) # each item: (node, its depth) # your code here Stuck? A hint The queue holds (node, depth) tuples. Pop one and unpack it. If both children are None , it's a leaf: return depth . Otherwise queue each existing child with depth + 1 . New words Queue A collection where items join at the back and leave from the front. FIFO First in, first out. deque Python's double-ended queue: O(1) append and popleft . Breadth-first search (BFS) Visiting nodes in order of distance from the start, using a queue. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. Why use deque.popleft() instead of list.pop(0) ? popleft is O(1); pop(0) is O(n) pop(0) removes the wrong item Lists can't hold tree nodes popleft also sorts the queue Removing a list's first item shifts all the others along. 2. A stack is LIFO. What is a queue? FIFO: first in, first out LIFO: last in, first out Sorted: smallest out first Random: any item out Like a queue at the bank, whoever arrived first leaves first. 3. In level-order BFS, what tells you how many nodes are on the current level? The queue's length when the level starts The depth of the tree The number of leaves Double the previous level's size At that moment the queue holds exactly one level; children added during it belong to the next. 4. Why can BFS stop at the first leaf in Minimum Depth? It meets nearer nodes before farther ones Leaves are always on the left The first leaf is the deepest It visits nodes in sorted order BFS goes level by level, so the first leaf found is on the shallowest level with a leaf. title: Heaps and priority queues
summary: Priority queues; the binary heap as a tree stored in a list where every parent is no bigger than its children (a min-heap); heapq.heappush, heapq.heappop (O(log n)), heap[0] to peek (O(1)), heapq.heapify (O(n)); making a max-heap by storing negatives; keeping a min-heap of size k for the k largest; tuples in heaps compared item by item; LeetCode 1046 Last Stone Weight, 215 Kth Largest Element in an Array, 973 K Closest Points to Origin.
text: Most urgent first In real life A hospital emergency room doesn't see patients in arrival order. The most urgent case is always seen next, even if they arrived last. And the nurse doesn't re-sort the whole waiting room whenever someone new comes in; they just need to know who's most urgent right now. A priority queue always gives you the item with the highest priority next. The usual way to build one is a heap . 1 In a min-heap , the smallest item is always at the top. It's a binary tree (Lesson 28) stored inside a plain list, with one rule: every parent is no bigger than its children. 2 That rule is much weaker than "fully sorted", which is why keeping it is cheap. Operation (module heapq ) Does Cost heapq.heappush(h, x) add x O(log n) heapq.heappop(h) remove and return the smallest O(log n) h[0] peek at the smallest O(1) heapq.heapify(h) turn an existing list into a heap, in place O(n) Costs and functions from the heapq documentation. 3 triage.py import heapq waiting = [5, 1, 8, 3] heapq.heapify(waiting) heapq.heappush(waiting, 2) print(heapq.heappop(waiting)) print(heapq.heappop(waiting)) print(waiting[0]) Shows 1 2 3 A max-heap from a min-heap Python's heapq only does min-heaps. To get the largest first, store negative numbers: the most negative is the smallest, which was originally the largest. Negate again when you take it out. LeetCode 1046: Last Stone Weight Each turn, smash the two heaviest stones together. Equal weights destroy both; otherwise the lighter one is destroyed and the heavier one's weight drops by the lighter's weight. Return the weight of the last stone left, or 0 if none are left. 4 Use a max-heap of negatives. import heapq class Solution: def lastStoneWeight(self, stones): heap = [-s for s in stones] heapq.heapify(heap) # your code here Stuck? A hint While there are at least two stones, pop twice (negating to get the real weights). If they differ, push back the negative of the difference. At the end, return -heap[0] if anything's left, else 0. The k largest, without sorting everything In real life Picking a team of the 3 tallest people in a stadium. You don't need to rank all 50,000 of them. Keep 3 people standing at the front. Each time someone taller than the shortest of your 3 comes along, the shortest sits down and the new person stands up. To find the k largest items, keep a min-heap of size k. For each number, push it; if the heap grows past k, pop the smallest. At the end, the heap holds the k largest, and its top, heap[0] , is the k-th largest. That's O(n log k), better than sorting's O(n log n) when k is small. LeetCode 215: Kth Largest Element in an Array Return the k-th largest number (counting duplicates: in [3, 3, 1], the 2nd largest is 3). Use a min-heap of size k, not sorting. 5 import heapq class Solution: def findKthLargest(self, nums, k): heap = [] # your code here Heaps of tuples Heaps compare items with < , and tuples compare item by item: first elements first, and only if those tie, the second elements. So you can push (priority, thing) pairs, and the heap orders them by priority. This is how you attach data to a priority. LeetCode 973 asks for the k points closest to (0, 0). 6 Distance from the origin is x*x + y*y under a square root, but the square root doesn't change which is closer, so skip it. Push (distance, x, y) tuples. LeetCode 973: K Closest Points to Origin Return the k points closest to (0, 0), in any order. Each point is a list [x, y] . import heapq class Solution: def kClosest(self, points, k): pass Stuck? A hint Simplest version: build a list of (x*x + y*y, x, y) tuples, heapify it, then pop k times and collect [x, y] . (The size-k heap from the last section is faster when k is small; try it once this passes.) New words Priority queue A queue that hands out the highest-priority item next. Min-heap A tree kept in a list where every parent is no bigger than its children, so the smallest is on top. heapq Python's module of heap functions on plain lists. Top-k pattern Keep a heap of size k to find the k largest or smallest items. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. In a Python heap h , where is the smallest item? h[0] h[-1] h[len(h) // 2] Anywhere: you must search heapq keeps the smallest at index 0, the top of the tree. 2. How do you make heapq give the largest item first? Push negative values Pass reverse=True Pop from the end Use heapq.maxpop() Negating flips the order, so the largest original value becomes the smallest stored one. 3. What's the cost of heappop on a heap of n items? O(log n) O(1) O(n) O(n log n) Restoring the heap rule moves an item down one path of the tree, about log n levels. 4. To find the 3rd largest of a million numbers, keep a min-heap of what size? 3 1,000,000 500,000 1 A size-k min-heap holds the k largest so far; its top is the k-th largest. title: Graphs
summary: Graphs as vertices and edges; directed and undirected; adjacency lists as a dictionary of lists built from an edge list; the visited set that stops infinite loops in cycles; DFS (recursive) and BFS (deque) on graphs; counting connected components; grids as graphs where each cell's neighbours are up, down, left and right; LeetCode 733 Flood Fill and 200 Number of Islands; O(V + E).
text: Things and connections In real life A map of towns joined by roads. Some towns have many roads, some only one. You can drive round in a circle and end up where you started. There's no "top" town the way a tree has a root. A graph is a set of vertices (also called nodes) joined by edges . Edges can be one-way, making a directed graph (like following someone on social media), or two-way, an undirected graph (like a friendship). 1 A tree is a graph with no cycles and one root; general graphs can have both cycles and disconnected pieces. The usual way to store one is an adjacency list : a dictionary from each vertex to a list of its neighbours. 2 Problems often hand you a list of edges, so building the dictionary is step one: roads.py edges = [("Lagos", "Ibadan"), ("Ibadan", "Ilorin"), ("Lagos", "Abeokuta")] graph = {} for a, b in edges: graph.setdefault(a, []).append(b) graph.setdefault(b, []).append(a) # undirected: both ways print(graph["Lagos"]) Shows ['Ibadan', 'Abeokuta'] graph.setdefault(a, []) gives the list for a , creating an empty one first if needed. Exploring without going round in circles In real life Exploring a maze, you chalk an X on every junction you've been to. Arriving at an X, you know not to go that way again, or you'd walk the same loop forever. DFS and BFS work on graphs just as on trees, with one addition: a visited set. Trees never lead back to a node you've seen; graphs with cycles do, so without the chalk marks you'd loop forever. 3 Each vertex is visited once and each edge looked at once (twice if undirected), so both are O(V + E) : vertices plus edges. 4 explore.py def dfs(graph, start, visited): visited.add(start) for neighbour in graph.get(start, []): if neighbour not in visited: dfs(graph, neighbour, visited) A connected component is a group of vertices that can all reach each other. To count them: go through every vertex; each time you find one not yet visited, that's a new component, so count it and explore everything reachable from it. Try it: count the groups of friends People are numbered 0 to n - 1 , and pairs lists who are friends. Return how many separate friend groups there are. Build an adjacency list, then count components with DFS. def count_groups(n, pairs): graph = {person: [] for person in range(n)} for a, b in pairs: graph[a].append(b) graph[b].append(a) visited = set() groups = 0 # your code here return groups Stuck? A hint Write a small explore(person) function inside, like dfs above. Then loop over everyone: when someone isn't in visited , add 1 to groups and explore them. A grid is a graph too In real life The paint bucket tool in a drawing app: click one pixel, and the colour spreads to every touching pixel of the same colour, and from those to theirs, until it reaches a different colour. Many graph problems never mention a graph. In a grid (Lesson 16), each cell is a vertex, and its neighbours are the cells up, down, left and right. The bounds checking you wrote for the Game of Life applies directly. Instead of a separate visited set, you can often change the cell itself (repaint it, or turn land into water) so you never count it twice. LeetCode 733: Flood Fill Starting at image[sr][sc] , repaint it and every connected cell of the same original colour (up, down, left, right) with color . Return the image. 5 class Solution: def floodFill(self, image, sr, sc, color): start = image[sr][sc] if start == color: return image def fill(r, c): pass # your code here fill(sr, sc) return image Stuck? A hint Inside fill : return straight away if (r, c) is off the grid or isn't the start colour. Otherwise paint it, then call fill on the four neighbours. LeetCode 200: Number of Islands grid holds "1" for land and "0" for water (strings). An island is land connected up, down, left or right. Count the islands. 6 It's the friend-groups problem on a grid: for each unvisited land cell, count it and sink the whole island. class Solution: def numIslands(self, grid): rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0]) islands = 0 # your code here return islands Stuck? A hint Write a sink(r, c) like fill , turning "1" into "0" . Then loop over every cell: on a "1" , add one island and sink it so its cells are never counted again. Very big grids Recursion depth is limited to about 1,000 calls (Lesson 25). For a huge island, a BFS with a deque (Lesson 29) avoids that limit: queue the starting cell, and queue each neighbouring land cell as you sink it. LeetCode's tests pass either way. New words Graph Vertices (things) joined by edges (connections). Directed / undirected Edges that go one way / both ways. Adjacency list A dictionary from each vertex to its list of neighbours. Connected component A group of vertices that can all reach each other. O(V + E) Time proportional to the number of vertices plus edges. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. Why does graph DFS need a visited set when tree DFS didn't? Graphs can have cycles Graphs are always bigger Graphs have no root node Sets make DFS run in O(1) A cycle leads back to a vertex you've seen; without marking it, you'd loop forever. 2. In an undirected adjacency list, the edge A-B is stored how? B in A's list and A in B's list Only B in A's list Only A in B's list As a separate key "A-B" Two-way edges are recorded from both ends. 3. In Number of Islands, which cells count as neighbours? Up, down, left and right All eight surrounding cells Only the cell to the right Any cell in the same row The problem connects land horizontally and vertically only, so diagonal land is a separate island. 4. The time cost of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges? O(V + E) O(V × E) O(V²) O(log V) Each vertex is visited once and each edge checked a constant number of times. title: Backtracking: try, undo, try again
summary: Backtracking as depth-first search over choices; the choose / explore / un-choose template with a shared path list and path.pop(); copying the path with path[:] when saving an answer; the decision tree; why these problems are exponential (2^n subsets, n! permutations); pruning with a used set and with a running total; LeetCode 78 Subsets, 46 Permutations, 39 Combination Sum.
text: Every path through the choices In real life Finding your way through a hedge maze: at each junction, pick a path. Hit a dead end? Walk back to the last junction and take the next path you haven't tried. Do that systematically and you'll eventually walk every route. Backtracking is a depth-first search (Lesson 28) over choices rather than over a data structure. 1 Picture a decision tree : at the root you've chosen nothing; each branch is one choice. Reaching the bottom of the tree means one complete answer. Backtracking walks every branch of that tree, recursively. Almost every backtracking solution uses the same three-step template, with one shared list, path , holding the choices made so far: 2 template.py def backtrack(...): if the path is a complete answer: results.append(path[:]) # save a COPY return for choice in the choices available now: path.append(choice) # 1. choose backtrack(...) # 2. explore path.pop() # 3. un-choose (backtrack) Two details that catch everyone: path.pop() after the recursive call undoes the choice, so the next loop iteration starts from the same state. That's the "back" in backtracking. Save path[:] , not path . A slice makes a new copy of the list. 3 Saving path itself saves a reference to the one shared list, which keeps changing, and ends up empty. Subsets: take it or leave it In real life Choosing pizza toppings from mushroom, onion and pepper. For each topping you decide yes or no. Three yes/no decisions give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 possible pizzas, including the plain one with nothing. For subsets, the choice at each item is "include it or not". With n items that's 2 n subsets, so any solution is O(2 n ) at least: there are simply that many answers to write out. 4 Exponential problems like this usually come with small inputs (LeetCode 78 has at most 10 numbers). One neat way: at position i , first explore with nums[i] added, then explore without it. When i reaches the end, the path is a complete subset. LeetCode 78: Subsets Return all subsets of nums (all numbers are different). Any order is fine. class Solution: def subsets(self, nums): results = [] path = [] def backtrack(i): if i == len(nums): results.append(path[:]) return # include nums[i], explore, undo # then explore without it backtrack(0) return results Stuck? A hint Four lines: path.append(nums[i]) , backtrack(i + 1) , path.pop() , backtrack(i + 1) . The first call explores "with", the second "without". Getting a list of empty lists? You saved path instead of path[:] . Every saved answer is the same list, which is empty by the end. Permutations: every ordering In real life Seating 3 guests in 3 chairs: anyone can take the first chair, then either of the 2 left takes the second, and the last person gets the last chair. 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 seating plans. A permutation is an ordering of all the items. Now the choice at each step is "which unused item goes next?", so keep a set of items already in the path and skip those. Skipping choices that can't lead to a valid answer is called pruning . With n items there are n! (n factorial, Lesson 25) orderings: 6 for 3 items, 3,628,800 for 10. LeetCode 46: Permutations Return all orderings of nums (all different). Any order is fine. class Solution: def permute(self, nums): results = [] path = [] used = set() def backtrack(): pass # your code here backtrack() return results Stuck? A hint Base case: len(path) == len(nums) , save a copy. Otherwise, for each n in nums not in used : append it and add it to used , call backtrack() , then undo both. Challenge: making a total LeetCode 39: find every combination of the given numbers that adds up to target , where each number can be used any number of times . 6 [2, 2, 3] and [7] both make 7 from [2, 3, 6, 7]. Two ideas keep it correct and fast. To avoid listing [2, 2, 3] and [3, 2, 2] as different answers, only ever choose numbers from the current position onwards (pass a start index). To prune, stop as soon as the remaining total goes below zero: adding more can only make it worse. LeetCode 39: Combination Sum Return all unique combinations (each as a list) of candidates that sum to target . Numbers may repeat within a combination. Any order is fine. class Solution: def combinationSum(self, candidates, target): results = [] path = [] def backtrack(start, remaining): pass # your code here backtrack(0, target) return results Stuck? A hint Base cases: remaining == 0 means save a copy; remaining < 0 means give up on this path. Loop for i in range(start, len(candidates)) , and recurse with backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i]) : passing i , not i + 1 , is what allows reusing the same number. New words Backtracking Building answers one choice at a time, undoing the last choice to try the next. Decision tree A picture of all the choices: each branch one choice, each bottom a complete answer. Permutation One ordering of all the items. n items have n! of them. Pruning Skipping branches that can't lead to a valid answer. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. Why save path[:] rather than path ? path keeps changing; the slice is a frozen copy path[:] is sorted automatically Python can't append a list to a list path[:] removes duplicate items There's only one path list. Without a copy, every saved answer points at it and changes with it. 2. How many subsets does a set of 5 different items have? 32 25 120 10 Each item is in or out: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. 3. What does path.pop() after the recursive call do? Undoes the choice to try the next one Returns the answer to the caller Removes duplicate answers Stops the search completely It restores the path to how it was before this choice: the backtrack step. 4. In Combination Sum, why recurse with i instead of i + 1 ? So the same number can be reused So the answers come out sorted To skip numbers already used Because i + 1 could go out of range Staying at i lets the next choice be the same number again. Starting at i, not 0, still prevents re-orderings. Submit, read, then practise from memory Submit on LeetCode Submit all three (links in Sources). title: Dynamic programming 1: remember, don't repeat
summary: Overlapping subproblems; memoisation (top-down) with a dictionary cache; tabulation (bottom-up) with a list filled from the smallest case; reducing space to two variables; the recurrence relation; Fibonacci in O(n); LeetCode 70 Climbing Stairs, 746 Min Cost Climbing Stairs, 198 House Robber (take it or skip it).
text: Write the answer down the first time In real life Someone asks you "what's 37 × 48?" You work it out on paper: 1776. Five minutes later they ask again. You don't redo the multiplication; you look at what you wrote down. Dynamic programming works the same way. Recursive Fibonacci was slow because fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3) , and fib(4) calls fib(3) again , and so on: the same subproblems (smaller versions of the problem) get solved many times. When that happens, the problem has overlapping subproblems , and dynamic programming (DP) applies: solve each subproblem once and store the answer. 1 The quickest way is memoisation : keep a dictionary (the cache ) from input to answer. Before computing, check the cache; after computing, store the result. 1 This is called top-down DP, because you start from the big question and recurse down. fast_fib.py cache = {} def fib(n): if n < 2: return n if n in cache: # seen it before? just look it up return cache[n] cache[n] = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) return cache[n] print(fib(80)) Shows (instantly) 23416728348467685 Each fib(k) is now computed once, so the whole thing is O(n) instead of O(2ⁿ). fib(80) without the cache would take longer than a human lifetime. Find the recurrence, then build up In real life Climbing stairs one or two steps at a time. How many different ways are there to reach step 10? Think about your very last move: you arrived either from step 9 (a single step) or from step 8 (a double step). So the ways to reach 10 are the ways to reach 9 plus the ways to reach 8. That sentence is a recurrence relation : the answer for n written in terms of answers for smaller n. 3 Finding it is the hard part of most DP problems. Here it's ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2) , with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2 . (Yes, it's Fibonacci in disguise.) Instead of recursing down, you can also start from the smallest cases and fill in a list upwards: tabulation , or bottom-up DP. No recursion, so no recursion limit. 1 table.txt step: 1 2 3 4 5 ways: 1 2 3 5 8 each = the two before it added LeetCode 70: Climbing Stairs Return the number of distinct ways to climb n steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Build it bottom-up; it must handle n = 45 instantly. class Solution: def climbStairs(self, n): if n <= 2: return n ways = [0] * (n + 1) ways[1], ways[2] = 1, 2 # fill in ways[3] to ways[n] return ways[n] You often only need the last two Each entry only looks at the two before it, so you don't need the whole list: two variables, rolled forward, give O(1) space. Get it right with a list first, then shrink it. DP for the cheapest way DP isn't only for counting. LeetCode 746 gives a cost for standing on each step; you can start on step 0 or 1 and climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. What's the cheapest way to get past the top? 4 Same reasoning about the last move, with min instead of + : the cheapest cost to reach step i is the cheaper of arriving from i - 1 or from i - 2, each plus that step's cost. LeetCode 746: Min Cost Climbing Stairs Return the minimum cost to reach the top (one step past the last index). class Solution: def minCostClimbingStairs(self, cost): n = len(cost) best = [0] * (n + 1) # best[i] = cheapest cost to stand on step i (step n is the top) # your code here return best[n] Stuck? A hint Starting on step 0 or 1 is free, so best[0] and best[1] stay 0. For i from 2 to n: best[i] = min(best[i-1] + cost[i-1], best[i-2] + cost[i-2]) . You pay a step's cost when you step off it. Challenge: take it or skip it In real life Picking fruit from a row of trees where an alarm goes off if you pick from two neighbouring trees. At each tree you decide: pick here (so you must have skipped the previous one), or skip it (and keep whatever you had by the previous tree). LeetCode 198 is the classic version: houses in a row with money in each, and you can't rob two neighbours. 5 For each house, the best total up to here is the better of two options: rob it (its money plus the best up to two houses back) or skip it (the best up to the previous house). That "take it or skip it" choice comes up in many DP problems. LeetCode 198: House Robber Return the most money you can take without robbing two neighbouring houses. Try it with two variables (O(1) space): prev2 is the best up to two houses back, prev1 the best up to the previous house. class Solution: def rob(self, nums): prev2, prev1 = 0, 0 for money in nums: pass # work out the best up to this house, then roll the two variables forward return prev1 Stuck? A hint Inside the loop: current = max(prev1, prev2 + money) (skip it, or take it). Then roll forward with the tuple trick from Lesson 14: prev2, prev1 = prev1, current . New words Dynamic programming (DP) Solving overlapping subproblems once each and reusing the answers. Memoisation Caching each function result the first time it's computed (top-down). Tabulation Filling a table from the smallest cases upwards (bottom-up). Recurrence relation A rule giving the answer for n in terms of answers for smaller inputs. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What makes a problem suitable for dynamic programming? The same subproblems come up repeatedly The input list is already sorted The answer is always a single number It can be solved with one loop Overlapping subproblems are what make storing answers pay off. 2. What's the difference between memoisation and tabulation? Top-down with a cache vs bottom-up with a table One uses lists, the other uses sets Memoisation is exponential, tabulation linear Tabulation only works for Fibonacci Both solve each subproblem once; they differ in direction. 3. With 1 or 2 steps at a time, how many ways are there to climb 4 steps? 5 4 6 8 ways(4) = ways(3) + ways(2) = 3 + 2. 4. In House Robber, the best total at a house is the larger of? Skip it, or its money plus best two back Its money, or the previous house's money The sum of all houses so far, or zero Best one back plus best two back Taking it forbids the neighbour, so it pairs with the best up to two houses back. title: Dynamic programming 2: grids and choices
summary: Two-dimensional DP tables built with list comprehensions; filling a grid where each cell depends on the cell above and to the left; using infinity (float('inf')) for impossible states; LeetCode 62 Unique Paths, 322 Coin Change (fewest coins, -1 if impossible), 1143 Longest Common Subsequence (match: diagonal + 1; no match: best of up or left); a five-step recipe for any DP problem.
text: A table instead of a row In real life A city laid out in a grid of streets. You walk from the top-left corner to the bottom-right, only ever going right or down. How many different routes are there? To reach any corner, your last step came either from the corner above or the corner to the left. That's LeetCode 62. 4 The recurrence: paths[r][c] = paths[r - 1][c] + paths[r][c - 1] . Every cell in the top row and left column has exactly one route (straight along the edge). Fill the rest row by row, and the bottom-right cell is the answer: O(rows × columns). grid.txt 3 rows by 4 columns: 1 1 1 1 1 2 3 4 1 3 6 10 <- 10 routes Build the table with a list comprehension (Lesson 16), never with [[1] * n] * m , which repeats one shared row. LeetCode 62: Unique Paths Return the number of routes from top-left to bottom-right of an m by n grid, moving only right or down. class Solution: def uniquePaths(self, m, n): paths = [[1] * n for _ in range(m)] # fill in every cell not in the top row or left column return paths[m - 1][n - 1] Fewest coins In real life A shopkeeper giving change wants to use as few coins as possible. Grabbing the biggest coin first usually works with real currencies, but not always: with coins of 1, 3 and 4, making 6 greedily gives 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), while 3 + 3 uses two. So try every coin, and remember answers. Let best[a] be the fewest coins that make amount a . For each amount, try each coin as the last one used: best[a] = min(best[a - coin] + 1) over all coins that fit. 1 best[0] is 0. Amounts you can't make start as infinity , float("inf") , which is bigger than any number, so min ignores them. 3 If best[amount] is still infinity at the end, return -1. 5 LeetCode 322: Coin Change Return the fewest coins needed to make amount (each coin can be used any number of times), or -1 if it's impossible. class Solution: def coinChange(self, coins, amount): best = [float("inf")] * (amount + 1) best[0] = 0 # your code here return best[amount] if best[amount] != float("inf") else -1 Stuck? A hint Two loops: amounts a from 1 to amount , and inside, each coin . If the coin fits ( coin <= a ), see whether best[a - coin] + 1 beats the current best[a] . Comparing two texts In real life Two people write down the same shopping list from memory. Some items match and appear in the same order, some are extra. The longest run of shared items in the same order shows how similar the lists are. Tools that show "what changed" between two versions of a file, like Git (Lesson 35), are built on this idea. A subsequence keeps some characters in order, possibly with gaps: "ace" is a subsequence of "abcde". LeetCode 1143 asks for the length of the longest one shared by two strings. 6 Make a table with a row for each prefix of text1 and a column for each prefix of text2 (plus an empty row and column of zeros). For each cell, compare the two current characters: They match: 1 + the cell diagonally up-left (both strings one shorter). They don't: the bigger of the cell above and the cell to the left (drop a character from one string or the other). LeetCode 1143: Longest Common Subsequence Return the length of the longest common subsequence of text1 and text2 . class Solution: def longestCommonSubsequence(self, text1, text2): rows, cols = len(text1), len(text2) table = [[0] * (cols + 1) for _ in range(rows + 1)] # fill table[i][j] for i in 1..rows and j in 1..cols # (the current characters are text1[i - 1] and text2[j - 1]) return table[rows][cols] Stuck? A hint Nested loops over i and j from 1. If text1[i - 1] == text2[j - 1] , the cell is table[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 ; otherwise max(table[i - 1][j], table[i][j - 1]) . A recipe for any DP problem Define the state in words: "best[a] is the fewest coins to make a". Everything follows from this sentence. Find the recurrence by thinking about the last choice: last step, last coin, last characters. Set the base cases : the smallest states, answered directly (0 coins for amount 0, one route along the edge). Choose an order so that every cell's ingredients are filled in before the cell itself. Read off the answer , then check the Big O: usually the number of states times the work per state. New words State What one cell of the DP table means, in words. float("inf") Infinity: larger than any number, used for "impossible so far". Subsequence Characters kept in order, gaps allowed: "ace" in "abcde". Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. In Unique Paths, each cell is filled from which cells? The one above and the one to the left The one below and the one to the right All eight neighbours Only the diagonal up-left You can only arrive by moving down (from above) or right (from the left). 2. Why does Coin Change start every amount at infinity? So unmakeable amounts never win a min() Because coins can be used forever To make the table use less memory Python lists must start at infinity Infinity means "impossible so far": any real count is smaller, and if it stays infinity the answer is -1. 3. Is "aec" a subsequence of "abcde"? No: the order is wrong Yes: all three letters appear Yes: gaps are allowed No: it isn't contiguous Gaps are allowed, but the characters must stay in the original order, and c comes before e. 4. What's the first step of the DP recipe? Define what a cell means in words Write the nested loops Fill the table with zeros Submit to see what fails A clear state definition is what makes the recurrence findable. title: Git and GitHub: save points and a portfolio
summary: Version control with Git: repositories, the working folder, staging with git add, commits as save points with messages, git status and git log; .gitignore for .venv and __pycache__; GitHub as an online home for repositories; creating a repository on GitHub and pushing with git remote add origin and git push -u origin main; the edit, add, commit, push loop.
concepts: git init / status / add / commit / log
text: Save points for your code In real life A video game with save points. Before the boss fight, you save. If it goes badly, you load the save instead of starting the whole game again. And you can look back at a list of every save, each with a note like "before the boss". Version control keeps a history of your project, so you can see what changed, when, and go back. Git is the version control tool almost every software team uses. 1 A folder whose history Git tracks is a repository (or "repo"). Each save point is a commit : a snapshot of your files plus a short message saying what changed. Saving happens in two steps. 1 First you choose which changes go in the next snapshot, called staging ( git add ). Then you take the snapshot ( git commit ). Like packing a box before sealing it: you decide what goes in, then tape it shut with a label. Check Git is installed. Terminal > git --version % git --version $ git --version Shows something like git version 2.55.0 .windows.2 Paste what your terminal showed: Git is installed. If Windows doesn't recognise git, install it from git-scm.com (the default options are fine), then open a new terminal window. If a box offers to install the command line developer tools, accept it: that installs Git. Then open a new terminal window. If it says command not found , install Git with your package manager (on Ubuntu: sudo apt install git ). Tell Git who you are (once per computer; it labels your commits). Use the email you'll use for GitHub: Terminal > git config --global user.name "Your Name" % git config --global user.name "Your Name" $ git config --global user.name "Your Name" > git config --global user.email "you@example.com" % git config --global user.email "you@example.com" $ git config --global user.email "you@example.com" Make a project and turn it into a repository. Each portfolio project gets its own folder and its own repo. From your course folder: Terminal ...python-course> mkdir projects\hello-git python-course % mkdir -p projects/hello-git python-course $ mkdir -p projects/hello-git ...python-course> cd projects\hello-git python-course % cd projects/hello-git python-course $ cd projects/hello-git ...hello-git> git init -b main hello-git % git init -b main hello-git $ git init -b main Shows Initialized empty Git repository in .../hello-git/.git/ Git keeps the whole history in a hidden .git folder inside the project. 2 -b main names the main line of history "main", which is what GitHub expects. Your first commit Make a file in the project, hello.py , containing print("hi") . Then ask Git what it sees: Terminal ...hello-git> git status hello-git % git status hello-git $ git status Shows On branch main No commits yet Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) hello.py "Untracked" means Git sees the file but isn't keeping its history yet. git status is the command you'll run most; it always tells you where you are and often suggests what to do next. 3 Ignore what shouldn't be saved. Virtual environments (Lesson 18) and Python's cache folders don't belong in a repo; anyone can recreate them. Make a file called .gitignore containing: .gitignore .venv/ __pycache__/ Git skips anything matching a line in .gitignore . 3 Stage and commit. git add . stages everything in the folder (the dot means "here"). -m gives the commit message: Terminal ...hello-git> git add . hello-git % git add . hello-git $ git add . ...hello-git> git commit -m "First commit" hello-git % git commit -m "First commit" hello-git $ git commit -m "First commit" ...hello-git> git log --oneline hello-git % git log --oneline hello-git $ git log --oneline Shows something like [main (root-commit) a60018f] First commit 2 files changed, 3 insertions(+) create mode 100644 .gitignore create mode 100644 hello.py a60018f First commit You may also see warnings about "LF will be replaced by CRLF". That's Git noting the different ways Windows and other systems end lines; it's harmless. The 7 characters like a60018f are the start of the commit's unique ID. Paste what git log --oneline showed: Your first save point exists. From now on, commit whenever something works. Run git status : if files are listed under "Changes to be committed", the commit didn't happen; if under "Untracked", run git add . first. A good commit message says what the change does, in a few words: "Add neighbour counting", "Fix crash on empty board". Commit small and often: each commit is a save point you can return to. GitHub: your code, online In real life Git is your notebook of save points, kept at home. GitHub is a public library shelf where you can put a copy. Employers can browse it, and if your laptop dies, your work is still there. GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories. Your GitHub profile becomes a portfolio: recruiters often look at it. 4 A copy of your repo somewhere else is called a remote ; sending your commits to it is a push . Make a GitHub account at github.com if you don't have one. Choose a professional username; it will appear in your portfolio links. Create an empty repository on GitHub: the + menu, then New repository . Name it hello-git , make it Public, and don't tick the options to add a README or .gitignore (your local repo already has files, and those options would create a conflicting first commit). 5 Connect and push. GitHub shows the commands on the new repo's page; they look like this, with your username: Terminal ...hello-git> git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/hello-git.git hello-git % git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/hello-git.git hello-git $ git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/hello-git.git ...hello-git> git push -u origin main hello-git % git push -u origin main hello-git $ git push -u origin main origin is the usual nickname for your GitHub copy. 5 The first push may open a browser window asking you to sign in to GitHub; that's Git's credential helper, and you only do it once. Refresh the GitHub page: your files are there. The loop from now on Edit, then git add . , then git commit -m "..." , then git push . After the first push, plain git push is enough. Every project in the next five lessons gets its own repo, pushed to GitHub, with a README.md file: a short description that GitHub shows on the repo's front page. 4 Write what the project does, how to run it, and what you learned. That page is what an employer reads first. New words Repository (repo) A project folder whose history Git tracks. Commit A saved snapshot of the project, with a message. Staging Choosing which changes go into the next commit ( git add ). .gitignore A file listing things Git should not track. Remote / push A copy of the repo elsewhere / sending your commits to it. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What's the right order to save your work? add, then commit, then push commit, then add, then push push, then add, then commit add, then push, then commit Stage the changes, take the snapshot, then send it to GitHub. 2. Why put .venv/ in .gitignore ? Anyone can recreate it; it's big and personal Git can't read files in .venv It contains your GitHub password It makes your code run faster Environments are rebuilt from a list of packages; committing them bloats the repo. 3. Which command tells you what Git currently sees? git status git push git init git remote status shows the branch, staged changes, unstaged changes and untracked files. 4. What does origin usually mean? Your repository's copy on GitHub The very first commit The folder you started Git in The main branch of history It's the conventional nickname for the remote you push to. Read, then practise Read next Pro Git: What is Git? About 15 minutes, free from Git's official site. Then Recording Changes to the Repository , which covers everything in this lesson in more depth. Before Lesson 36 Put your practice folder under Git: git init -b main inside it, a .gitignore , and a first commit. Push it to a new GitHub repo called python-practice . Every exercise you've written since Lesson 2 is now saved. Stuck? Ask your tutor With the course app running, press Ask your tutor and paste any Git message you don't understand.

title: Project: Conway's Game of Life
summary: Robert Heaton's Game of Life project: board as a grid of 0s and 1s; dead_state(width, height); the rules (underpopulation, survival, overpopulation, reproduction) in next_cell_value; next_board_state built into a new board so updates don't interfere; render to text; random_state; an animation loop with time.sleep and ANSI clear-screen codes; still lifes and oscillators (block, blinker) as test cases; packaging the project in its own repo with a README.
concepts: new board vs updating in place
text: Life, by four rules In real life Imagine a town where every house is either lived in or empty, and each night the same rules decide what happens: a lonely household moves out, an overcrowded one moves out, a comfortable one stays, and an empty house with exactly three neighbouring families attracts a new one. Run it night after night and surprisingly lifelike patterns appear. Conway's Game of Life is a grid of cells , each alive (1) or dead (0). Every step, all cells update at once, based on how many of their 8 neighbours are alive: 1 A live cell with 0 or 1 live neighbours dies (underpopulation). A live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours stays alive. A live cell with more than 3 live neighbours dies (overpopulation). A dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours becomes alive (reproduction). This project comes from the Project Based Learning list, Robert Heaton's "Programming Projects for Advanced Beginners". 1 2 His page breaks it into milestones; this lesson follows them, with tests for each piece. You already wrote the hardest part, live_neighbours , in Lesson 16; it's provided below so every exercise can use it. Milestone 1: an empty board Write dead_state(width, height) returning a board of height rows, each with width zeros. Each row must be its own list (remember the shared-row trap from Lesson 16). def dead_state(width, height): pass Milestone 2: the rules for one cell Write next_cell_value(cell, neighbours) : given a cell's current value (0 or 1) and how many live neighbours it has, return its value in the next step, by the four rules above. def next_cell_value(cell, neighbours): pass Milestone 3: the next board All cells must update at the same time . If you change cells in the board while you're still counting neighbours on it, later cells see a half-updated board and get the wrong count. So build a brand-new board for the next step, reading only from the old one. Two famous patterns make perfect tests. A 2 by 2 block never changes (a still life). A line of three, a blinker , flips between horizontal and vertical every step (an oscillator). 1 Milestone 3: next_board_state Write next_board_state(board) returning a new board one step later. Use live_neighbours and next_cell_value (both already written for you above your code). def next_board_state(board): height = len(board) width = len(board[0]) new_board = [[0] * width for _ in range(height)] # your code here return new_board Milestone 4: render it as text Write render(board) returning one string: each row on its own line, # for alive and . for dead. Rows are joined with "\n" (a new-line character) and there's no new line at the very end. def render(board): pass Put it together on your computer Now the real program, with an animation in your terminal. Each piece goes in one file, with the functions you just wrote. Make the project and its repo (Lesson 35): Terminal ...python-course> mkdir projects\game-of-life python-course % mkdir -p projects/game-of-life python-course $ mkdir -p projects/game-of-life ...python-course> cd projects\game-of-life python-course % cd projects/game-of-life python-course $ cd projects/game-of-life ...game-of-life> git init -b main game-of-life % git init -b main game-of-life $ git init -b main ...game-of-life> code life.py game-of-life % code life.py game-of-life $ code life.py Write life.py : paste in your dead_state , live_neighbours , next_cell_value , next_board_state and render , then add these at the bottom: life.py (the end) import random import time def random_state(width, height): board = dead_state(width, height) for r in range(height): for c in range(width): if random.random() < 0.3: # about 30% of cells start alive board[r][c] = 1 return board def run(width=60, height=20, generations=200): board = random_state(width, height) for step in range(generations): print("\033[H\033[J", end="") # clear the terminal screen print(render(board)) print(f"Generation {step}") board = next_board_state(board) time.sleep(0.1) if __name__ == "__main__": run() random.random() gives a decimal between 0 and 1, so it's below 0.3 about 30% of the time. 4 time.sleep(0.1) pauses a tenth of a second between frames. 3 The odd string "\033[H\033[J" is a special code that tells the terminal to clear the screen, so each frame replaces the last. Run it : python python3 life.py . Patterns grow, collide and settle into blocks and blinkers. Press Ctrl + C to stop early. Paste the last line your program printed: It's alive. Now make it yours with the extensions below, then publish it. If you see a NameError, one of the functions wasn't pasted into life.py, or is below the code that uses it. Make it yours (pick at least one) Heaton's page suggests extensions; they're what turns a tutorial into a portfolio piece. 1 Load a pattern from a file : read a text file of . and # into a board, so you can start from a glider or a "Gosper glider gun". Wrap around the edges : make cells on the right edge neighbours of cells on the left, using % (Lesson 6) on the row and column. Stop when stable : end the loop when the next board equals the current one, and print how many generations it took. Publish it Write README.md in the project folder, in plain text: README.md # Game of Life Conway's Game of Life in the terminal, written in Python with no libraries. ## Run it python life.py ## How it works The board is a list of lists of 0s and 1s. Each step builds a new board, counting each cell's 8 neighbours and applying the four rules. ## What I learned (Write two or three sentences in your own words.) Commit and push : git add . , git commit -m "Game of Life" , create an empty game-of-life repo on GitHub, then git remote add origin ... and git push -u origin main as in Lesson 35. Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. A dead cell with 3 live neighbours. Next step? It becomes alive It stays dead It dies twice Its neighbours die Exactly three live neighbours is the reproduction rule. 2. Why build a new board instead of updating the old one cell by cell? Later cells would count already-updated neighbours Python lists can't be changed after creation A new board makes the program run faster The render function needs two boards All cells must update together, based only on the previous step. 3. What is a blinker? A line of three that flips each step A square of four that never changes A cell that is born and dies at once A pattern that moves across the board It's the simplest oscillator: horizontal, vertical, horizontal... 4. What's the Big O of one step on a w by h board? O(w × h) O(w + h) O((w × h)²) O(1) Each of the w × h cells checks a fixed 8 neighbours. title: Project: an unbeatable Tic-Tac-Toe AI
summary: Robert Heaton's Tic-Tac-Toe AI project: a 3x3 board as a list of lists with None, X and O; get_winner checking rows, columns and diagonals; legal_moves; the minimax algorithm scoring a position +10 / -10 / 0 by exploring every future move recursively, maximising on the AI's turn and minimising on the opponent's; place, recurse, undo (backtracking); best_move; a human-versus-AI game loop in the terminal; README and GitHub.
text: A board and a referee In real life Before any clever play, a game needs a board and a referee who can say "that square's taken" and "X wins". This project follows Robert Heaton's two-part brief from the Project Based Learning list. 1 2 3 The board is a 3 by 3 grid (Lesson 16) holding "X" , "O" , or None for an empty square. Milestone 1: who has won? Write get_winner(board) returning "X" or "O" if that player has three in a row (any row, column or diagonal), otherwise None . 1 def get_winner(board): lines = [] # add the 3 rows, the 3 columns and the 2 diagonals to lines, # each as a list of 3 values, then check each line return None Stuck? A hint A row is board[i] ; a column is [board[0][i], board[1][i], board[2][i]] ; the diagonals use positions (0,0),(1,1),(2,2) and (0,2),(1,1),(2,0). A line wins if its first value isn't None and all three are equal: a == b == c works in Python. Milestone 2: legal moves Write legal_moves(board) returning a list of (row, col) tuples for every empty square, in reading order (top row first, left to right). def legal_moves(board): pass Minimax: imagine every future In real life A careful chess player thinks: "If I move here, what's my opponent's best reply? And then my best answer to that?" They assume the opponent always plays as well as possible, and choose the move whose worst outcome is the best. With noughts and crosses, the game is small enough to imagine every possible future. Minimax gives each position a score from the AI's point of view: +10 if the AI has won, -10 if it has lost, 0 for a draw. 2 For a position that isn't finished, try every legal move, score the position each one leads to (recursively, Lesson 25), and then: on the AI's turn, take the highest score (it picks its best move); on the opponent's turn, take the lowest (assume they play their best too). Trying a move means: place it, recurse, then remove it again. That's exactly the choose / explore / un-choose of backtracking (Lesson 32). The tree of all possible games is called the game tree . shape.txt minimax(board, player to move, ai): if someone has won: return +10 if it's ai, else -10 if no moves are left: return 0 for each legal move: place it score = minimax(board, the other player, ai) remove it return the biggest score if player is ai, else the smallest Milestone 3: minimax and best_move Finish minimax(board, player, ai) and best_move(board, ai) . best_move tries each legal move for the AI, scores it with minimax (the opponent moves next), and returns the move with the highest score. get_winner and legal_moves are already written for you. def minimax(board, player, ai): winner = get_winner(board) if winner is not None: return 10 if winner == ai else -10 moves = legal_moves(board) if not moves: return 0 scores = [] # for each move: place player's mark, score it, undo return max(scores) if player == ai else min(scores) def best_move(board, ai): best, best_score = None, -100 # try each legal move for ai, score it with minimax(board, other(ai), ai) return best Hint 1: minimax's loop for r, c in moves: then board[r][c] = player , scores.append(minimax(board, other(player), ai)) , board[r][c] = None . Hint 2: "Board is unchanged" fails Every place you put a mark to try it, you must set it back to None straight after, in both functions. Play against it Set up the project : projects/tic-tac-toe , git init -b main , and a file tictactoe.py containing get_winner , legal_moves , other , minimax and best_move . Add a board printer and a game loop at the bottom: tictactoe.py (the end) def render(board): print(" 0 1 2") for r in range(3): cells = [board[r][c] or "." for c in range(3)] print(r, " ".join(cells)) def ask_move(board): while True: text = input("Your move as row col (like 1 2): ").split() if len(text) == 2 and text[0].isdigit() and text[1].isdigit(): r, c = int(text[0]), int(text[1]) if 0 <= r < 3 and 0 <= c < 3 and board[r][c] is None: return r, c print("That's not a free square. Try again.") def play(): board = [[None] * 3 for _ in range(3)] human, ai = "X", "O" turn = "X" while get_winner(board) is None and legal_moves(board): render(board) if turn == human: r, c = ask_move(board) else: r, c = best_move(board, ai) print(f"AI plays {r} {c}") board[r][c] = turn turn = other(turn) render(board) winner = get_winner(board) print(f"{winner} wins!" if winner else "It's a draw.") if __name__ == "__main__": play() board[r][c] or "." shows a dot for empty squares, because None counts as false. ask_move keeps asking until the input is a free square: the input validation loop from Lessons 7 and 15. Play : python python3 tictactoe.py . Try to win. You can't: the best you can do is draw. Paste the last line of a finished game: The AI held. Minimax with perfect play never loses at noughts and crosses. If X won, there's a bug: check that minimax maximises on the AI's turn and minimises on yours, and that every trial move is undone. Make it yours (pick at least one) Let the human choose X or O , and who goes first. Prefer faster wins : score a win as 10 - depth , so the AI wins in as few moves as possible instead of playing with its food. Count positions : add a counter of how many times minimax is called for the first move. Then look up "alpha-beta pruning" and see how much it saves. The lowest The highest The average The first one found It assumes the opponent plays their best, which is the worst for the AI. 2. Why remove each trial mark after scoring it? So the next trial starts from the same board To make the board print correctly Because Python lists can't hold None So the AI forgets the opponent's moves Place, recurse, undo: the backtracking pattern from Lesson 32. 3. What does minimax return for a finished game the AI lost? -10 10 0 None Scores are from the AI's point of view: a loss is -10. 4. What does None or "." evaluate to? "." None True False or gives the first value that counts as true; None counts as false, so it gives ".".
