title: Project: Snake in the terminal
summary: Robert Heaton's Snake project: the snake as a list of (row, col) tuples with the head first; directions as (row change, col change) in a dictionary; moving by adding a new head and dropping the tail unless food was eaten; detecting death by walls or self-collision; blocking reverse turns; separating game logic from drawing; a real-time loop with curses (windows-curses on Windows) using a timeout so the game ticks without key presses; installing the package in a virtual environment; README and GitHub.
concepts: snake as a list of tuples
text: A snake is a list of squares In real life A conga line moving across a dance floor: the leader steps forward, and everyone else takes the place of the person in front. From above, it looks like the whole line moved one step, but really a new square was taken at the front and one was given up at the back. This project is from Robert Heaton's series in the Project Based Learning list. 1 5 The key design choice, which he stresses, is keeping the game logic (where the snake is, what happens next) separate from the display (drawing it on screen). The logic is plain Python you can test here; the display comes at the end. The snake is a list of (row, col) tuples, head first: [(5, 4), (5, 3), (5, 2)] is a snake of length 3 facing right. Directions are small steps: "UP" is one row up, (-1, 0) ; "RIGHT" is one column right, (0, 1) . Moving one tick: work out the new head, put it at the front, and remove the last square, unless the new head lands on the food. Then the tail stays, and the snake is one square longer. Milestone 1: move and grow Write move(snake, direction, food) . Return a tuple (new_snake, ate) : the snake after one tick, and True if it ate the food. Don't change the list you were given; build a new one. DIRECTIONS = {"UP": (-1, 0), "DOWN": (1, 0), "LEFT": (0, -1), "RIGHT": (0, 1)} def move(snake, direction, food): head_r, head_c = snake[0] dr, dc = DIRECTIONS[direction] new_head = (head_r + dr, head_c + dc) # your code here Stuck? A hint [new_head] + snake is a new list with the head added. If it ate, return that. Otherwise drop the last square with a slice: [new_head] + snake[:-1] . Dying, and no U-turns The snake dies if its head goes off the board or onto its own body. It also shouldn't be able to reverse straight back into itself: pressing left while moving right should be ignored. 1 Milestone 2: game over? Write is_dead(snake, height, width) : True if the head is outside rows 0 to height - 1 or columns 0 to width - 1 , or if the head is somewhere in the rest of the body. def is_dead(snake, height, width): pass Milestone 3: no reversing Write is_opposite(new, current) returning True if the two directions are opposites (UP and DOWN, or LEFT and RIGHT). def is_opposite(new, current): pass A tidy way A dictionary from each direction to its opposite, then return opposites[new] == current . Make it real-time In real life A metronome ticks whether or not you play a note. Snake works the same way: every tick the snake moves, and pressing a key only changes the direction for the next tick. input() waits for Enter, which is no good for a game that keeps moving. The curses library takes over the terminal window: it reads single key presses, can wait a set time for one and carry on if none comes, and draws characters anywhere on the screen. 2 Windows needs one extra package for it, windows-curses , which you'll install in a virtual environment (Lesson 18). 4 Set up the project : Terminal ...python-course> mkdir projects\snake python-course % mkdir -p projects/snake python-course $ mkdir -p projects/snake ...python-course> cd projects\snake python-course % cd projects/snake python-course $ cd projects/snake ...snake> git init -b main snake % git init -b main snake $ git init -b main ...snake> python -m venv .venv snake % python3 -m venv .venv snake $ python3 -m venv .venv ...snake> code requirements.txt snake % code requirements.txt snake $ code requirements.txt Put this one line in requirements.txt and save it. It tells pip to install windows-curses on Windows only, because Mac and Linux already have curses: requirements.txt windows-curses; sys_platform == "win32" Then install what it lists, and add a .gitignore with the line .venv/ : Terminal ...snake> .venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt snake % .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt snake $ .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt Create snake.py with DIRECTIONS , move , is_dead and is_opposite from above. Create game.py , the display and keyboard part: game.py import curses import random from snake import move, is_dead, is_opposite HEIGHT, WIDTH = 15, 30 KEYS = {curses.KEY_UP: "UP", curses.KEY_DOWN: "DOWN", curses.KEY_LEFT: "LEFT", curses.KEY_RIGHT: "RIGHT"} def place_food(snake): while True: spot = (random.randrange(HEIGHT), random.randrange(WIDTH)) if spot not in snake: return spot def draw(screen, snake, food, score): screen.erase() screen.addstr(0, 0, "+" + "-" * WIDTH + "+") for r in range(HEIGHT): screen.addstr(r + 1, 0, "|" + " " * WIDTH + "|") screen.addstr(HEIGHT + 1, 0, "+" + "-" * WIDTH + "+") screen.addstr(food[0] + 1, food[1] + 1, "*") for r, c in snake: screen.addstr(r + 1, c + 1, "O") screen.addstr(HEIGHT + 2, 0, f"Score: {score} (arrow keys to steer, q to quit)") screen.refresh() def main(screen): curses.curs_set(0) # hide the cursor screen.timeout(120) # getch waits at most 120 ms: one tick snake = [(7, 10), (7, 9), (7, 8)] direction = "RIGHT" food = place_food(snake) score = 0 while True: draw(screen, snake, food, score) key = screen.getch() # -1 if no key was pressed this tick if key == ord("q"): # ord() turns a letter into the number getch() reports for that key break if key in KEYS and not is_opposite(KEYS[key], direction): direction = KEYS[key] snake, ate = move(snake, direction, food) if is_dead(snake, HEIGHT, WIDTH): break if ate: score += 1 food = place_food(snake) return score if __name__ == "__main__": final = curses.wrapper(main) print(f"Final score: {final}") curses.wrapper(main) sets the terminal up, runs main , and always puts the terminal back to normal afterwards, even if your code crashes. 2 screen.timeout(120) is the metronome: getch() returns a key if one is pressed within 120 milliseconds, or -1 if not, and the loop moves on either way. 3 Play with the environment's Python, in a terminal window at least 50 characters wide and 20 lines tall: Terminal ...snake> .venv\Scripts\python game.py snake % .venv/bin/python game.py snake $ .venv/bin/python game.py After a game, paste the line it printed: A real-time game, written by you. Now make it yours and publish it. An error mentioning addwstr or addstr usually means the terminal window is too small: make it bigger and run again. ModuleNotFoundError: No module named '_curses' means plain python python3 ran instead of .venv\Scripts\python .venv/bin/python . Make it yours (pick at least one) Speed up : lower the timeout a little every time the snake eats. Wrap-around walls : instead of dying at the edge, come out the other side (use % ). High score : save the best score to a text file and show it on screen (reading and writing files is in ATBS chapter 10 ). Then write the README (include the pip install step, using requirements.txt ), commit, and push it as terminal-snake . Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. When the snake eats, what's different about the move? The tail isn't removed The head isn't added The snake moves two squares The direction is reversed Adding a head and keeping the tail makes it one square longer. 2. Why use screen.timeout(120) rather than waiting for a key? So the snake moves even with no key pressed So the screen refreshes more slowly So only arrow keys are accepted To limit the game to 120 moves getch gives up after 120 ms and returns -1, so every loop is one tick of the game. 3. Why keep the game logic in a separate file from the curses code? So the logic can be tested without a screen Because curses can't import functions So the game runs twice as fast Because Python allows one function per file Plain functions in, plain values out: easy to test, as you did on this page. 4. How does is_dead detect the snake biting itself? The head is in the rest of the body The snake is longer than the board Two keys were pressed at once The tail is next to the head snake[0] in snake[1:] checks whether the head shares a square with any body part. title: Project: build your own calculator language
summary: Following Ruslan Spivak's Let's Build A Simple Interpreter parts 1 to 6: an interpreter reads text and carries it out; a lexer (tokenizer) turns characters into tokens such as INT, PLUS, LPAREN, EOF, reading multi-digit numbers and skipping spaces; a grammar with expr, term and factor encoding precedence (* and / before + and -, parentheses first); a recursive-descent parser in a class with eat(); left-to-right evaluation of chains; raising ValueError for invalid input; a read-eval-print loop (REPL).
text: Teaching a computer to read maths In real life Reading a sentence happens in two steps you rarely notice. First you split the letters into words ("the", "cat", "sat"). Then you work out how the words fit together: who did what. A program that understands a language does the same two steps, just much more strictly. An interpreter is a program that reads text written in some language and carries it out. Python itself is one. This project follows Ruslan Spivak's series "Let's Build A Simple Interpreter", from the Project Based Learning list, through its first six parts: a calculator that understands + - * / , order of operations and brackets. 1 5 The lexer (or tokenizer) splits text into tokens : meaningful pieces like "the number 12" or "a plus sign", skipping spaces. 1 The parser reads the tokens following the rules of the language, called its grammar , and works out the answer. Step 1: characters into tokens Each token here is a tuple: its kind and its value. "12 + 3" becomes [("INT", 12), ("PLUS", "+"), ("INT", 3), ("EOF", None)] . The final EOF ("end of file") token marks the end, so the parser knows when to stop. 1 A number can be several digits long, so keep reading digits until a non-digit appears. Milestone 1: tokenize Write tokenize(text) . Kinds: INT (value is the whole number), PLUS , MINUS , MUL , DIV , LPAREN , RPAREN (value is the character), and a final ("EOF", None) . Skip spaces. Any other character: raise ValueError(f"Unexpected character: {ch}") . SYMBOLS = {"+": "PLUS", "-": "MINUS", "*": "MUL", "/": "DIV", "(": "LPAREN", ")": "RPAREN"} def tokenize(text): tokens = [] i = 0 while i < len(text): ch = text[i] # spaces, digits (possibly several), symbols, or an error i += 1 tokens.append(("EOF", None)) return tokens Reading a whole number When ch.isdigit() , remember start = i , then move i forward while the characters are digits. int(text[start:i]) is the number. In that branch, i has already moved past it, so don't add 1 again (use if / elif branches, each moving i itself). Step 2: a grammar that knows the order of operations In real life A shopping receipt: the total is a sum of lines; each line is a quantity times a price; and a "price" might be a bundle in brackets that you work out first. Sums are made of products, products are made of single items or bracketed bundles. That nesting is exactly how maths precedence works. Ruslan writes the grammar as three rules, each built from the next: 3 4 grammar.txt expr : term ((PLUS | MINUS) term)* term : factor ((MUL | DIV) factor)* factor : INT | LPAREN expr RPAREN Read * as "zero or more times" and | as "or". An expr is terms added or subtracted; a term is factors multiplied or divided; a factor is a number or a whole expression in brackets. Because term sits inside expr , multiplications are finished before additions see them: precedence falls out of the shape. And because factor refers back to expr , brackets can nest as deep as you like. A recursive descent parser turns each rule into one method. 3 A helper, eat(kind) , checks the current token is the kind expected and moves on, or raises an error if it isn't. Each rule's loop handles a chain like 7 - 3 - 2 from left to right, so it means (7 - 3) - 2. 2 In this calculator / is whole-number division, // , so every answer stays an int . Milestone 2: the parser Finish factor , term and expr . calc(text) is already written: it parses one expr and then insists the next token is EOF , so leftover tokens like the 3 in "2 3" are an error. tokenize is already written for you. class Parser: def __init__(self, tokens): self.tokens = tokens self.pos = 0 def current(self): return self.tokens[self.pos] def eat(self, kind): token = self.current() if token[0] != kind: raise ValueError(f"Expected {kind} but found {token[0]}") self.pos += 1 return token def factor(self): # INT, or LPAREN expr RPAREN pass def term(self): # factor, then any number of (MUL or DIV) factor pass def expr(self): # term, then any number of (PLUS or MINUS) term pass def calc(text): parser = Parser(tokenize(text)) result = parser.expr() parser.eat("EOF") return result Hint 1: factor If the current token is LPAREN : eat it, get value = self.expr() , eat RPAREN , return value . Otherwise return the number: self.eat("INT")[1] (eat returns the token, and [1] is its value). If it isn't an INT, eat raises the error for you. Hint 2: term and expr term : value = self.factor() , then while self.current()[0] in ("MUL", "DIV"): eat the operator and combine value with the next self.factor() . expr is the same shape one level up, with term , PLUS and MINUS . Your own language prompt The Python shell from Lesson 2 is a REPL : Read a line, Evaluate it, Print the result, Loop. Yours is a few lines. 1 Set up projects/calculator with git init -b main , and put SYMBOLS , tokenize , Parser and calc in calc.py . Add the loop at the bottom: calc.py (the end) def repl(): print("Calculator. Type an expression, or quit to leave.") while True: text = input("calc> ").strip() if text == "quit": break if not text: continue try: print(calc(text)) except ValueError as error: print(f"Error: {error}") except ZeroDivisionError: print("Error: division by zero") if __name__ == "__main__": repl() except ValueError as error keeps the error so you can show its message (Lesson 15). Run it with python python3 calc.py and type 2 + 3 * (4 - 1) . Paste what it printed for 2 + 3 * (4 - 1) : Correct: 3 times 3 first, then add 2. Your parser respects precedence and brackets. If you got 15, multiplication isn't binding tighter than addition: check that expr calls term , and term calls factor . Make it yours (pick at least one) Negative numbers : let a factor be a minus sign followed by another factor, so -3 + 5 and 2 * -(1 + 1) work. (That's Ruslan's part 7 and 8 territory.) Variables : support x = 5 then x * 2 , storing names in a dictionary. Show the tokens : a :tokens 2+3 command that prints the token list, which makes debugging much easier. Then write the README (include the grammar), commit, and push as python-calculator-interpreter . Check yourself From memory, without scrolling up. A wrong answer here costs nothing: you just pick again. 1. What does the lexer produce? A list of tokens The final answer A list of characters The grammar rules It groups characters into meaningful pieces; the parser does the rest. 2. Why does 2 + 3 * 4 give 14 and not 20? term sits inside expr, so * finishes first The lexer sorts the tokens by operator Python's own maths overrides the parser expr reads the tokens from right to left expr asks term for its pieces, and term has already done the multiplication. 3. What does eat("RPAREN") do if the current token is INT ? Raises a ValueError Skips the INT token Returns None quietly Inserts a bracket eat insists on the expected kind; anything else is a syntax error. 4. What does REPL stand for? Read, evaluate, print, loop Run every Python line Repeat each parse later Return each printed line Read a line, work it out, show the result, and go round again. Read, then reflect Read Ruslan Spivak: Let's Build A Simple Interpreter, parts 1 to 6 Read them in order now; you'll recognise every idea. His versions use a class for the lexer too, and draw "syntax diagrams" for each rule, which are worth copying into your README. Later parts build a real Pascal interpreter, a good long-term follow-on project. Before Lesson 40 Draw the grammar's three rules as boxes on paper, then trace (1 + 2) * 3 through them by hand, writing down each method call in order. Stuck? title: Project: write your own Git
summary: Following Write yourself a Git and Pro Git's Git Objects chapter: content-addressed storage; bytes versus str and .encode(); a blob object is the header blob <size>, a zero byte, then the content; its ID is the SHA-1 hash in hex (hashlib.sha1().hexdigest()); objects live in .git/objects/<first two hex>/<other 38>, compressed with zlib; reading an object back by decompressing and splitting at the zero byte; a command-line tool with sys.argv; writing objects that the real git cat-file can read.
text: A filing system labelled by content In real life Imagine a library where every book's shelf label is calculated from the book's exact words. Two identical copies always get the same label, so the library only ever keeps one. Change a single comma and the label is completely different. You can find any book instantly if you know its label, and you can check a book hasn't been tampered with by recalculating it. Git stores every version of every file like that. A file's contents are turned into a 40-character ID by a hash function called SHA-1, and the file is saved under that ID. This is called content-addressed storage . 2 The stored file is called a blob object. Those commit IDs like a60018f from Lesson 35 are the start of hashes too. This project follows "Write yourself a Git", from the Project Based Learning list, which rebuilds Git's core in Python, together with the Pro Git chapter on Git's objects. 1 2 6 Today: the blob, hashing, storing and reading back. Bytes, not text Hashing and compression work on raw bytes , not on Python strings. A bytes value is written with a b before the quote: b"hello" . Convert text to bytes with "hello".encode() and back with .decode() . A byte with value zero, written b"\x00" , is how Git separates the header from the content. The blob format and its ID Git doesn't hash the content alone. It first adds a short header: the word blob , a space, the content's length in bytes, and a zero byte. For content b"hello\n" (6 bytes), the full object is b"blob 6\x00hello\n" . Its SHA-1 hash, written as 40 hex characters, is the blob's ID. 2 3 Milestone 1: blob bytes and hash Write blob_bytes(data) returning the header plus content, and hash_object(data) returning the 40-character hex ID, using hashlib.sha1(...).hexdigest() . The tests compare against IDs the real Git produces. import hashlib def blob_bytes(data): # b"blob " + the length as bytes + b"\x00" + data pass def hash_object(data): pass Stuck? A hint The length is a number: turn it into text with str() , then into bytes with .encode() . Bytes join with + just like strings. For the hash: hashlib.sha1(blob_bytes(data)).hexdigest() . Where and how objects are saved Git saves each object inside the repo's .git/objects folder: the first two characters of the ID name a sub-folder, and the other 38 name the file. So ce0136... lives at .git/objects/ce/013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a . Splitting by the first two characters keeps any one folder from holding millions of files. 2 The file isn't stored as plain bytes: it's compressed with zlib , using zlib.compress() , and read back with zlib.decompress() . 2 4 Milestone 2: path, pack and unpack Write object_path(sha) returning the path as a string with forward slashes. Write read_object(stored) : decompress the stored bytes, split at the first zero byte, and return a tuple (kind, content) , where kind is the header's first word as text (like "blob" ) and content is the bytes after the zero byte. blob_bytes is already written for you. import zlib def object_path(sha): pass def read_object(stored): raw = zlib.decompress(stored) # split raw at the first b"\x00" into header and content # the header looks like b"blob 6": its first word is the kind pass Splitting only once raw.split(b"\x00", 1) splits at the first zero byte only, so content that itself contains zero bytes survives. Then header.split(b" ")[0].decode() gives "blob" . A command-line tool the real Git agrees with Real tools take instructions from the command line: git hash-object hello.txt . In Python, the words typed after the script's name arrive in the list sys.argv : python python3 mygit.py hash-object hello.txt gives ["mygit.py", "hash-object", "hello.txt"] . 5 Make a playground repo (a throwaway one, so experiments can't harm a real project): Terminal ...python-course> mkdir projects\mygit python-course % mkdir -p projects/mygit python-course $ mkdir -p projects/mygit ...python-course> cd projects\mygit python-course % cd projects/mygit python-course $ cd projects/mygit ...mygit> git init -b main mygit % git init -b main mygit $ git init -b main Write mygit.py with blob_bytes , hash_object , object_path and read_object , then this at the bottom: mygit.py (the end) import os import sys def write_object(data): sha = hash_object(data) path = object_path(sha) os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True) with open(path, "wb") as f: f.write(zlib.compress(blob_bytes(data))) return sha def main(): command, filename = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2] if command == "hash-object": with open(filename, "rb") as f: data = f.read() if "-w" in sys.argv: print(write_object(data)) else: print(hash_object(data)) elif command == "cat-file": with open(object_path(filename), "rb") as f: kind, content = read_object(f.read()) print(content.decode(), end="") else: print(f"Unknown command: {command}") if __name__ == "__main__": main() Three new tools here. open(path, "rb") opens a file to r ead b ytes, and "wb" to write them; the with block closes the file for you afterwards. os.makedirs(..., exist_ok=True) creates the sub-folder if it's missing. Reading and writing files is covered properly in ATBS chapter 10 . Compare with the real Git.
